codes.document_title: IoD Code of Conduct for Directors
codes.notes: Voluntary code for all directors. Six principles: Leading by Example, Integrity, Transparency, Accountability, Fairness, Responsible Business. Developed by 16-member commission chaired by Lord McNicol.

codes.document_title: CMI Code of Conduct and Practice
codes.notes: Binding on all CMI members under Royal Charter. Covers competence, professionalism, honesty, integrity. Reviewed by Board of Trustees every 3 years. Members restate commitment annually.

Guides directors, officers, employees, chapter leaders. Emphasizes honesty, integrity, transparency, accountability, responsible stewardship. Supported by Conflicts of Interest Policy and Whistleblower Protection Policy.

codes.document_title: Academy of Management Code of Ethics
codes.notes: Covers research, teaching, practice, and service. Includes General Principles, Professional Principles, and enforceable Ethical Standards. Violations may lead to membership termination.

codes.document_title: AMA Code of Ethics and Conduct (Certified Professional in Management)
codes.notes: Required for AMA-CPM credential holders. Electronic signing required as part of certification. Non-compliance can result in credential revocation.

codes.document_title: Sarbanes-Oxley Act Section 406 — Code of Ethics for Senior Financial Officers
codes.notes: Mandatory disclosure requirement for public companies. Applies to principal executive officer, principal financial officer, controller. Requires codes promoting honest conduct, proper disclosure, legal compliance. Waivers must be disclosed on Form 8-K.

codes.organization: Institute of Management Consultants USA (IMC USA)
codes.notes: Required for all members and Certified Management Consultants (CMC). Covers objectivity, fees, third-party commissions, confidentiality. Members must report violations.

codes.organization: International Council of Management Consulting Institutes (ICMCI)
codes.notes: First international code of conduct for any profession (1989). Covers client confidentiality, unrealistic expectations, commissions, competency requirements. Renewed every 3 years with recertification.

minor_groups.name: Advertising, Marketing, Promotions, Public Relations, and Sales Managers

codes.notes: Core values: honesty, responsibility, equity, transparency, citizenship. Aspirational norms: do no harm, foster trust, embrace ethical values. Supported by AMA Code of Conduct with enforcement procedures.

Six core values: advocacy, honesty, expertise, independence, loyalty, fairness. Six code provisions covering honest communication, fair competition, confidentiality, conflicts of interest. Professional obligation for all members.

Consolidates 1961 Code of Venice, 1965 Code of Athens, 2007 Code of Brussels. 18 articles grounded in UN Declaration of Human Rights. Reviewed 2020, no changes needed. AI-specific PR guidelines added.

Emphasizes truthfulness, substantiation, fair competition, transparency in endorsements, privacy, and non-discrimination. Distinguishes advertising from editorial content. Voluntary but widely recognized.
Updated January 2025. Condition of membership. Covers ethical conduct, authenticity, transparency, regulatory compliance. Royal Charter since 1989. First Code of Practice introduced 1973.
International code for all SMEI certified professionals (CSE, CME, SCPM, SCPS). Founded 1935. Emphasizes consumer sovereignty, mutual benefit in transactions, highest professional standards.
Companion to the Sales Code. Covers marketing-specific ethical standards for marketing executives. Required for Certified Marketing Executive (CME) and Certified Professional Marketer designations.

For talent development professionals including training managers. Emphasizes rights and dignity, quality education, copyright compliance, confidentiality. Public declaration of obligations to profession and society.

Originally developed 1972 for HR professionals. Core principles: professional responsibility, ethical leadership, fairness and justice, conflicts of interest, use of information. The premier HR professional body in the US.

codes.organization: Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development (CIPD)
codes.document_title: CIPD Code of Conduct and Ethics
codes.notes: Effective 1 January 2023, replacing 2012 code. Royal Charter demands compliance regardless of grade/role. Core values: positive impact on working lives, civic virtue, stewardship, good character, professional competence.

codes.document_title: PMI Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct
codes.notes: Updated effective 17 November 2025. Core values: honesty, responsibility, respect, fairness. Includes aspirational and mandatory standards. Applies to all PMI members, volunteers, certification holders. Ethics Review Committee enforces.

codes.document_title: Principles and Standards of Ethical Supply Management Conduct
codes.notes: Three foundational principles: integrity, value, loyalty. Standards cover perceived impropriety, conflict of interest, undue influence, employer responsibilities, supplier relationships, confidentiality, reciprocity, legal compliance, professional competence.

codes.organization: Chartered Institute of Procurement and Supply (CIPS)
codes.notes: Binding under Royal Charter. Prohibits gifts/gratuities from suppliers. Duty to eradicate unethical practices from supply chain (human rights abuses, fraud, corruption). CIPS Ethical Procurement Certificate required for Chartered Status.

Applies to CSCP, CPIM, CLTD certification holders. Prohibits misrepresentation of qualifications. Non-compliance may result in decertification. Also developed SCOR-E framework covering ethical, economic, ecological dimensions.
Covers confidentiality, professional standards, fair dealing, conflict of interest, accountability. All members expected to comply. Board of Directors approves enforcement procedures.

For IT governance, audit, control, security, risk management professionals. Applies to CISA, CISM, CRISC, CGEIT holders. Covers standards support, professional performance, stakeholder service, confidentiality, professional education.

codes.organization: Society of Corporate Compliance and Ethics (SCCE)
codes.document_title: Code of Professional Ethics for Compliance and Ethics Professionals
codes.notes: Adopted 2007. Covers overarching principles and rules of conduct. Not legally binding but self-disciplinary mark of commitment. Applies to all compliance and ethics professionals (CEPs).

For regulatory and financial crime compliance professionals globally. 160,000+ professionals trained since 2001. Requires 35 hours CPD annually. Breaches trigger investigation and disciplinary hearing.

codes.organization: Chartered Institute of Logistics and Transport (CILT)
codes.notes: Founded 1919. Chartered body for logistics, transport, supply chain, operations management. Professional conduct code for MILT, CMILT, FCILT members. Promotes ethical standards in logistics and supply chain.

Establishes public trust in contract management process. Core principles: integrity and accountability, professional development, truthfulness, respect and diversity. Violations subject to disciplinary action including revocation of certification.

codes.document_title: APS Code of Professional Ethics and Professional Conduct
codes.notes: Required for CPP and CPPM certification. Covers employer loyalty, legal compliance, sound business principles, professional development. Adherence ensures public confidence in purchasing profession.

codes.organization: NIGP: The Institute for Public Procurement
codes.notes: Condition of membership. Covers public sector procurement specifically. Prohibits gifts/gratuities from suppliers. Emphasizes merit-based personnel decisions, confidential information protection, supplier relationships.

Applies to all AICP members. Comply with letter and spirit of insurance regulation laws. Abstain from conflicts of interest. Strive to improve regulatory compliance system. Includes Ethics 101 training course.

Global professional body for property/real estate management. Rules cover honest/fair/transparent conduct, due skill and care, clear terms, conflicts of interest, fair communication. Applies to all members and regulated firms.

Required for CIPP/CIPM/CIPT certification holders. Underpins professional conduct for privacy officers. The privacy profession has ongoing debate about whether a more comprehensive standalone code is needed.

For healthcare financial management professionals. Covers honesty, personal integrity, avoidance of conflicts of interest, fair financial presentation, confidentiality. Includes healthcare-specific ethical considerations.
Required for CCP, CBP, GRP, WLCP certification holders. Total rewards, compensation, and benefits professionals. Adherence required for maintaining certification status.
For training and development managers. Emphasizes rights and dignity of individuals, highest quality education/training, copyright compliance, professional development, confidentiality.

For HR specialists (13-1071). Originally 1972. Professional responsibility, ethical leadership, fairness and justice, conflicts of interest, information use. SHRM-CP and SHRM-SCP certification linked.

codes.organization: Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development (CIPD)
codes.document_title: CIPD Code of Conduct and Ethics
codes.notes: For HR specialists internationally. Royal Charter body. 2023 revision for modern working environment. Core values include positive impact on working lives, civic virtue, personal responsibility.

codes.document_title: PMI Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct
codes.notes: For management analysts using project management (13-1111). Four core values with aspirational and mandatory standards. PMP certification holders must comply.

codes.organization: Institute of Management Consultants USA (IMC USA)
codes.notes: For management analysts/consultants (13-1111). Condition of CMC certification. Covers objectivity, employee recruitment restrictions, fee transparency, third-party commissions, whistleblowing duty.

codes.organization: International Council of Management Consulting Institutes (ICMCI)
codes.notes: International standard for management consultants. First international professional code of conduct (1989). Covers legal, social, ecological aspects. Renewed with re-certification every 3 years.

codes.organization: Society of Corporate Compliance and Ethics (SCCE)
codes.document_title: Code of Professional Ethics for Compliance and Ethics Professionals
codes.notes: For compliance officers (13-1041). Overarching principles plus specific rules of conduct. Self-disciplinary commitment. Applies to CCEP certification holders.

International compliance professionals. Embodies principles of compliance/regulation upheld internationally. 35 hours CPD annually for Professional and Fellow members. Infringements trigger investigation.

codes.organization: Association for Financial Counseling and Planning Education (AFCPE)
codes.notes: For Accredited Financial Counselors (AFC). Annual signing required. Covers credibility, competency, honesty, integrity, limitations awareness. Violations may lead to suspension or revocation of certification.

Founded 1896 specifically to establish a code of ethics for credit professionals. Covers integrity, trust, fairness, confidentiality of credit information, lawful conduct. Required for NACM certified professionals.

For training and development specialists (13-1151). Professional obligations to self, profession, and society. Covers rights/dignity, quality standards, copyright, continuing education, confidentiality.

For contract specialists and buyers. Creates public trust in contract management process. Integrity, accountability, professional development, truthfulness, respect and diversity. Violations may result in revocation of membership/certification.

codes.document_title: Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct
codes.notes: Global benchmark for investment professionals since 1960s. Seven standards: professionalism, capital markets integrity, client duties, employer duties, investment analysis, conflicts, CFA responsibilities. Sanctions include designation revocation.

codes.organization: American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA)
codes.notes: Codified version effective December 15, 2014. Three parts: public accounting, business/industry, other members. Covers independence, integrity, objectivity, client confidentiality, conflicts. Used as basis for all state CPA regulations.

codes.organization: International Ethics Standards Board for Accountants (IESBA/IFAC)
codes.document_title: International Code of Ethics for Professional Accountants
codes.notes: 2025 Handbook edition. Global standard adopted by IFAC member bodies worldwide. Five fundamental principles: integrity, objectivity, professional competence/due care, confidentiality, professional behaviour. Conceptual framework approach for threat evaluation.

codes.document_title: IMA Statement of Ethical Professional Practice
codes.notes: Central code for management accountants. Updated 2017 from 2005 version. Overarching principles: Honesty, Fairness, Objectivity, Responsibility. Four standards: Competence, Confidentiality, Integrity, Credibility. Anonymous helpline available.

codes.document_title: CIMA Code of Ethics for Professional Accountants
codes.notes: Issued January 2020. Based on IESBA Code (Parts 1-3) with Part 2 co-developed with AICPA. Applies to all CIMA members and CGMA holders worldwide. Duty to observe highest standards of conduct and integrity.

codes.organization: Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales (ICAEW)
codes.notes: Latest version effective 1 July 2025. Five fundamental principles: integrity, objectivity, professional competence/due care, confidentiality, professional behaviour. Covers public practice, business, audit independence, insolvency.

codes.document_title: Global Internal Audit Standards — Domain II: Ethics and Professionalism
codes.notes: Former standalone Code of Ethics now integrated as Domain II of Global Internal Audit Standards (2024). Covers integrity, objectivity, confidentiality, competency. Applies to IIA members, certification holders, and all performing internal audit.

codes.organization: Chartered Institute of Internal Auditors (Chartered IIA)
codes.notes: UK/Ireland counterpart to IIA global standards. Principles-based, applied proportionately. Updated September 2024, effective January 2025. Based on IPPF and Global Internal Audit Standards. Non-adherence triggers disciplinary procedures.

All ACFE members must abide. Covers integrity, due professional care, critical analysis, professional skepticism. Fraud examinations must be legal, professional, thorough. Includes client communication standards at engagement start.

codes.document_title: Code of Ethics and Standards of Conduct
codes.notes: Effective October 1, 2019. Fiduciary duty is cornerstone. Principles: integrity, objectivity, competence, fairness, confidentiality. CFP Board monitors compliance and publishes disciplinary information.
Responsibilities to public, clients, colleagues, employers. Core values: integrity, objectivity, competence, diligence. Members must not subordinate candor to personal gain.

codes.organization: National Association of Personal Financial Advisors (NAPFA)
codes.document_title: NAPFA Fiduciary Oath and Code of Ethics
codes.notes: Fee-only fiduciary standard since 1983. Fiduciary oath: clients' interests first at all times. Code requires objectivity, confidentiality, competence, fairness, integrity, full disclosure, professionalism.

For FRM and ERP certification holders, Board, Regional Directors, staff. Covers professional integrity, personal accountability, best practice standards, honesty, confidentiality, objectivity. Cultural sensitivity provision. Violations may result in permanent FRM removal.
For alternative investment professionals. Covers professionalism, integrity, competence, confidentiality. Periodic reaffirmation required. Ethics integrated into Level I and Level II curriculum.

codes.organization: Society of Actuaries (SOA) / American Academy of Actuaries
codes.document_title: Code of Professional Conduct (Joint Actuarial Code)
codes.notes: Jointly adopted by all five US actuarial organizations (SOA, CAS, Academy, ASEA, CCA). Effective January 1, 2001. Precepts cover honesty, competence, qualifications, public responsibility. Material violations subject to counseling and discipline.

Revised version effective 25 September 2025. Six principles: Integrity, Competence and care, Impartiality, Compliance, Speaking up, Communication. Applies at all times in actuarial roles. Non-compliance triggers disciplinary proceedings.
For Certified Treasury Professional (CTP) and FP&A credential holders. Covers competence, professional duty, confidentiality, overall conduct. CTPs subject to credential revocation for violations.
For CGFM certification holders. Four principles: Accountability, Integrity and Professionalism, Objectivity, Confidentiality and Responsibility. Applies to all members and non-member CGFMs.

codes.document_title: NAEA Code of Ethics and Rules of Professional Conduct
codes.notes: For Enrolled Agents (tax representation before IRS). Layered with Treasury Circular 230. CPE requirements exceed IRS minimums. Honest, intelligent, ethical representation of taxpayer financial positions.

Threefold responsibility: to clients, to self, to government. Members must protect client interests, maintain professional reputation, comply with tax laws. Membership includes Ethics course and business practice webinars.

codes.document_title: ACM Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct
codes.notes: Adopted by ACM Council on June 22, 2018; replaces 1992 version. Organized in four sections: General Ethical Principles, Professional Responsibilities, Professional Leadership Principles, and Compliance. Over 100,000 members worldwide. Covers all computing professionals.

codes.organization: IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers)
codes.notes: Policy 7.8; originally adopted 1990, revised and approved by Board of Directors November 2020. 10 principles. Over 400,000 members in 160+ countries. Applies to all IEEE members including computer and software engineers.

codes.document_title: Software Engineering Code of Ethics and Professional Practice
codes.notes: Version 5.2; developed by IEEE-CS/ACM Joint Task Force on Software Engineering Ethics and Professional Practices (SEEPP), led by Don Gotterbarn. Eight principles: Public, Client & Employer, Product, Judgment, Management, Profession, Colleagues, Self. Standard for teaching and practicing software engineering.

codes.organization: ISC2 (International Information System Security Certification Consortium)
codes.notes: Four mandatory canons for CISSP and other certification holders. All ISC2 members must commit to the Code. Violations may result in revocation of certification. Over 600,000 members. In 2026, ISC2 also launched a broader Code of Professional Conduct for all cybersecurity professionals.

codes.organization: ISACA (Information Systems Audit and Control Association)
codes.notes: Applies to all ISACA members and certification holders (CISA, CISM, CRISC, CGEIT, CDPSE). Covers objectivity, due diligence, confidentiality, competence, transparency, and stakeholder education. Over 170,000 members in 188 countries.

codes.organization: BCS, The Chartered Institute for IT
codes.notes: Four key principles: public interest, professional competence, adherence to legal authority, and promoting integrity. Standards exceed general law. Enforced through disciplinary action up to expulsion. Royal Chartered body. Over 60,000 members.

Applies to all CompTIA certification holders (A+, Security+, Network+, etc.). Prohibits dishonesty, fraud, unauthorized system access, exam cheating. Violations may lead to sanctions or certification revocation.

codes.document_title: Data Science Code of Professional Conduct
codes.notes: Professional conduct creed for data science professionals. Addresses data privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency, and responsible use of data science techniques.

All IET members agree to abide by Rules of Conduct; re-affirmed annually. Covers electrical, electronic, computing, and information technology professionals. Over 150,000 members worldwide. Enforced through disciplinary regulations.

codes.document_title: Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct
codes.notes: Four core values: responsibility, respect, fairness, honesty. Contains both aspirational and mandatory standards. Updated version effective November 17, 2025. Over 700,000 members. Applies to all PMI credential holders (PMP, etc.). Included here as project management spans IT occupations (SOC 15-1299).

Originally issued 1982; revised 2016 and 2022. Eight topic areas: Professionalism, Responsibilities to Funders/Clients/Employers, Responsibilities in Publications and Testimony, Responsibilities to Research Subjects, Responsibilities to Other Statisticians, Responsibilities Regarding Allegations of Misconduct, Responsibilities of Employers, and Responsibilities of Mentors. Over 18,000 members.

codes.document_title: AMS Policy Statement on Ethical Guidelines
codes.notes: Set forth by AMS Council. Covers plagiarism, attribution, conflicts of interest, diversity, peer review, and editorial responsibilities. Enforced by Committee on Professional Ethics (COPE). Over 28,000 members.
Organizational code focusing on governance, whistleblower protection, and non-retaliation. Also addresses values of equity, diversity, and human flourishing in mathematics. Over 25,000 members.

codes.organization: SIAM (Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics)
codes.notes: Organizational code of conduct promoting inclusive climate, open exchange of ideas, and ethical behavior. Applies to all members and anyone acting on behalf of the organization. Over 14,000 members.

codes.document_title: AIA Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct
codes.notes: First adopted 1909; current version effective February 1, 2024. Three-tier structure: Canons (broad principles), Ethical Standards (aspirational goals), Rules of Conduct (mandatory). Canons cover general obligations, public, clients, profession, colleagues, and environment. Enforced by National Ethics Council. Over 98,000 members.

codes.organization: NCARB (National Council of Architectural Registration Boards)
codes.notes: Established 1977; serves as national model for state licensing boards. Five focus areas: competence, conflict of interest, full disclosure, compliance with laws, and signing/sealing documents. Annual certification required for NCARB Certificate holders.
Three core principles: integrity, competence, and relationships. Violations subject to disciplinary action including expulsion. Current version effective May 1, 2019.

Foundation of professional practice. Contains Canons with Ethical Standards (aspirational goals) and Rules (mandatory; violations trigger complaints). Covers duties to clients, employers, employees, and fellow professionals. ASLA also maintains a separate Code of Environmental Ethics.

Seven canons covering public duty, jurisdiction rules, competence, impartiality, confidentiality, proper advertising, and professional integrity. Preamble pledges service before profit. Over 15,000 individual members.

codes.organization: NCEES (National Council of Examiners for Engineering and Surveying)
codes.notes: Section 240.15 Rules of Professional Conduct. Provides licensure boards with guidelines for engineering and surveying licensing laws and ethics. Most recent version August 2025. Covers both professional engineers and professional surveyors.

codes.organization: ASPRS (American Society for Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing)
codes.notes: Founded 1934. Principles of honesty, justice, and courtesy. Covers photogrammetry, remote sensing, GIS, and geospatial disciplines. Obligations to employer, clients, and colleagues. Applies to over 7,000 members and certification holders.

Created 1946 (Canons of Ethics for Engineers); revised July 2019. Six Fundamental Canons: safety/health/welfare paramount, competence, truthful statements, faithful agents, avoid deceptive acts, honorable conduct. Board of Ethical Review (est. 1950s) issues advisory opinions. Foundational code referenced across all engineering disciplines.

First adopted 1914; completely rewritten October 26, 2020 (first wholesale update since 1974). New hierarchical stakeholder model: society, natural/built environment, profession, clients/employers, peers. Replaces former canon structure. Over 150,000 members.

Based on fundamental principles of integrity, honor, and dignity. Canons include: public safety paramount, competence, truthful statements, faithful agents, intellectual property, environmental sustainability. All ASME members agree to abide. Over 85,000 members.

Revised by Board of Directors in 2015. 11 principles covering public safety, environment, competence, faithful service, conflicts of interest, fair treatment, and equity/diversity/inclusion. Over 60,000 members.

codes.organization: IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers)
codes.notes: Policy 7.8; originally adopted 1990, revised 2020. 10 principles covering safety, conflicts of interest, honesty, discrimination, competence, and continuous improvement. Over 400,000 members in 160+ countries. Cross-listed with 15-1200 (Computer Occupations).

codes.organization: AIAA (American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics)
codes.notes: Adopted May 9, 2013; updated June 8, 2023. Covers public safety, lawful/ethical conduct, integrity, fair treatment. Reports to AIAA Ethics Committee. Over 30,000 members in aerospace engineering.

Primary principle: safety, health, welfare of public and fellow workers paramount. Covers environmental protection, sustainable development, conflicts of interest, faithful agency, continuing professional development. Over 10,000 members.

Required for all Registered Members. First duty: community welfare, health, and safety. Covers professional integrity, competence, fair competition, faithful agency, and truthfulness. Member society of AIME. Over 13,000 members.

codes.document_title: SPE Code of Conduct for Members
codes.notes: Guide for Professional Conduct approved by Board of Directors February 25, 1985. Covers integrity, societal responsibility, public health and safety, environmental responsibility, competence, and continuous learning. Member society of AIME. Over 130,000 members in 140+ countries.

codes.organization: ASHRAE (American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers)
codes.notes: Members pledge honesty, fairness, courtesy, competence, integrity, respect. Covers public health and safety, environmental stewardship, competence, conflicts of interest, confidentiality, and non-discrimination. Over 57,000 members.

Covers honesty, impartiality, integrity, knowledge currency, competence, and support for professional societies. Duties to society include environment/safety/welfare protection, risk management, and systems-level responsibility. Over 20,000 members.

Applies to Board members, officers, volunteers, staff, vendors, and consultants. Highest standards of legal, ethical, and moral conduct. Covers automotive, aerospace, and commercial vehicle industries. Over 200,000 members/volunteers.

codes.organization: AMPP (Association for Materials Protection and Performance)
codes.notes: Formed 2021 from merger of NACE International (corrosion engineers, est. 1943) and SSPC (protective coatings). Professional ethics for corrosion and materials protection. Includes certification ethics requirements and ethics training courses.

Released at General Assembly, October 14, 2023. Model code for member organizations worldwide. Covers integrity, competence, leadership, environmental protection. Aligned with UN Sustainable Development Goals. Represents 30 million engineers through ~100 national members.

codes.document_title: Code of Ethics and Guidelines on Professional Conduct
codes.notes: Four core values: integrity, competence, leadership, sustainability. Accountable under General Regulations 2016. Revised November 2019 and 2022. Over 100,000 members.

codes.document_title: Guideline on the Code of Ethics
codes.notes: Non-binding national synthesis of provincial/territorial regulators' codes. Updated July 2024 by Canadian Engineering Qualifications Board (CEQB). Dynamic principles rather than prescriptive rules. Represents 295,000 licensed engineers.

UK-based professional body for civil engineers. Covers integrity, competence, public interest, environmental responsibility, CPD. Companion Advice on Ethical Conduct updated December 2023. Over 95,000 members.
New Code launched January 1, 2022. Members required to abide by Code and undertake annual CPD. Subscribers to Statement of Ethical Principles. Guidance on ethics also available. Royal Chartered body.

Approved by Board of Trustees October 3, 2019. All members agree to abide; re-affirmed annually. Covers electrical, electronic, computing, manufacturing, and information technology professionals. Over 150,000 members worldwide. Cross-listed with 15-1200.

codes.organization: NCEES (National Council of Examiners for Engineering and Surveying)
codes.notes: Section 240.15 Rules of Professional Conduct for licensees. Guidelines for state engineering licensing boards. Most recent version August 2025. Cross-listed with 17-1000. Covers continuing professional competency and ethics awareness.

minor_groups.name: Drafters, Engineering Technicians, and Mapping Technicians

codes.notes: Eight principles: public safety paramount, competence, continuing development, faithful agency, quality products/services, associate with reputable organizations, objective/truthful statements, and uphold professional dignity. Enforced by Board of Directors with Board of Governors as appeals committee.

codes.organization: NICET (National Institute for Certification in Engineering Technologies)
codes.notes: Subsidiary of NSPE. Covers public safety, competence, quality of work, continuous improvement, and professional integrity. All applicants, candidates, and certificants must comply. Complements NSPE/NICET Code of Conduct. Certifications in fire protection, transportation, construction, industrial, and other engineering technology fields.

codes.organization: ASPRS (American Society for Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing)
codes.notes: Applies to mapping scientists, technologists, and interns. Principles of honesty, justice, and courtesy. Covers photogrammetry, remote sensing, GIS. Cross-listed with 17-1000 (Cartographers).
Engineering technicians and technologists who are NSPE members are also bound by this code. Six Fundamental Canons. Cross-listed with 17-2000 (Engineers). NICET operates as subsidiary of NSPE.

Amended May 2021. Guiding principles for all ESA members and certified ecologists. Covers scientific integrity, publication ethics, responsible professional practice, and public communication. Encourages ecological research and education and facilitating application of ecological science in management of ecological systems.

Approved by SCB Board of Governors July 29, 2004, accepted by membership August 1, 2004. Promotes dissemination of conservation knowledge, advocacy for reliable scientific methodology in management decisions, respectful treatment of colleagues, and protection of research subjects' rights. Foundational ethics code for conservation biology.

Umbrella ethics policy for AIBS employees, members, and volunteers. Requires honesty, compliance with laws, renunciation of scientific fraud and misconduct, and civil/respectful professional interactions. Includes whistleblower protections. AIBS is a nonprofit federation of scientific societies and organizations representing about 100 professional societies.

codes.document_title: ASM Code of Ethics and Conduct
codes.notes: Covers integrity and dignity of the microbial sciences profession. Members expected to be honest, ethical, impartial and professional. Includes unique biosecurity provision: members obligated to discourage any use of microbiology contrary to human welfare, including biological weapons. Ethics review process for reported breaches.

codes.organization: American Society for Biochemistry and Molecular Biology (ASBMB)
codes.document_title: ASBMB Code of Ethics and Conduct
codes.notes: Upholds integrity and dignity of biochemistry and molecular biology. Requires honest, ethical, impartial and professional interactions. Addresses conflict of interest, professional misconduct, abuse of privileged positions, and power differentials. Members take responsibility to report breaches.

codes.document_title: Code of Ethics and Conflict of Interest
codes.notes: First adopted 1985, last revised November 2012. Holds credible science as fundamental to all toxicological research. Requires objectivity, integrity, honesty, and truthfulness. Recognizes duty to communicate health, safety, and toxicity information responsibly. Full membership restricted to those with significant published work.

codes.organization: American Society of Naturalists / Society for the Study of Evolution / Society of Systematic Biologists
codes.notes: Collaboratively developed by three evolutionary biology societies. Covers research and publication ethics (data integrity, authorship, plagiarism), workplace conduct (anti-discrimination, anti-harassment, anti-retaliation), and enforcement procedures with sanctions for severe breaches. Underwent expert legal review.

codes.organization: American Society of Agronomy / Crop Science Society of America / Soil Science Society of America (ASA-CSSA-SSSA)
codes.document_title: Statement of Ethics and Code of Conduct
codes.notes: Joint statement of ethics for three allied agronomic sciences societies. Updated 2024 with companion Code of Conduct (2025). Values include integrity, diversity/equity/inclusion, scientific knowledge dissemination, and responsibility for economic, social, and environmental sustainability. Members and awardees must abide.

codes.organization: American Association for Laboratory Animal Science (AALAS)
codes.notes: Established 1950. Promotes highest level of ethics within laboratory animal science. Believes humane and responsible care of laboratory animals is vital to quality research. Administers three-tiered technician certification (ALAT, LAT, LATG) with embedded ethical standards. While not a standalone code, ethical expectations are woven into certification requirements.

codes.organization: American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS)
codes.document_title: Statement on Scientific Freedom and Responsibility
codes.notes: Adopted by AAAS Board October 12, 2017. Defines scientific freedom (freedom to inquire, pursue knowledge, communicate openly) as inextricably linked to scientific responsibility (duty to conduct science with integrity, in the interest of humanity, with respect for human rights). Cross-disciplinary statement applicable to all life and physical scientists. AAAS has promoted scientific ethics since the 1970s.

codes.document_title: The Chemical Professional's Code of Conduct
codes.notes: First approved by ACS Council March 16, 1994, replacing The Chemist's Creed (1965). Most recently updated August 28, 2019. Four pillars: scientific integrity (accurate records, no fabrication/falsification/plagiarism), professional conduct (anti-discrimination, anti-harassment), responsibility and accountability (duty to report misconduct), and professional development (lifelong learning, mentoring).

Scientific enterprise rests upon two ethical pillars: obligation to tell the truth (no fabrication, falsification, plagiarism) and obligation to treat people well (no abuse of power, fair and respectful relationships). Expanded and updated 2003. Comprehensive framework covering research integrity, mentoring, and professional interactions.

codes.document_title: Code of Conduct for APS Activities
codes.notes: Sets behavioral expectations governing APS members, non-members, staff, contractors, exhibitors, and sponsors at APS programs and activities. Designed to promote positive interactions within the physics community and with the public. Enforced through APS ethics procedures with investigation of violations.

codes.document_title: Scientific Integrity and Professional Ethics Policy
codes.notes: Built on the internationally recognized Singapore Statement (2010 World Conference on Research Integrity). Groundbreaking inclusion of harassment, discrimination, and bullying within the definition of research misconduct. Updated 2017 and 2023. Governs all AGU members, staff, volunteers, contractors, and sponsors. Ethics Committee investigates allegations with preponderance-of-evidence standard.

Originally adopted 1999, significantly updated. Addresses professional responsibility, integrity and accountability, respect for colleagues, public communication with clarity and accuracy, earth stewardship, and promotion of inclusive working environments free from harassment. AGI represents a federation of 52 geoscience societies.

codes.document_title: Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct
codes.notes: First mandatory code of ethics in GSA's 131-year history. Updated January 2023 to extend applicability to award recipients who are non-members. Guards against research misconduct, discrimination, harassment, and bullying. Enforceable with disciplinary sanctions. Since 2019, six members found in violation with sanctions imposed.

codes.document_title: AMS Code of Conduct and Ethical Guidelines
codes.notes: Core values: inclusion, objectivity, honesty, openness, fairness, respect, accountability. Adopts definition of scientific integrity as adherence to professional practices, ethical behavior, and principles of honesty, objectivity, and transparency. Committee on Ethics promotes high standards. Includes publication ethics policies and data access standards.

Guidelines and best practices for professional behavior in AAS activities and astronomical work broadly. Emphasizes mutual trust based on honest behavior. Code of Ethics Committee (CoEC) appointed 2016 to promote ethical conduct, oversee complaint investigations, and supervise mediation or recommend sanctions. Anti-harassment and non-discrimination policies.

Endorsed by AAG Council October 18, 1998; most recently revised June 12, 2024. Unusually broad scope spanning natural and social sciences, humanities, and arts. Unique provisions addressing military/intelligence funding concerns, environmental ethics obligations regarding anthropogenic environmental change, and well-being of more-than-human lives.

For radiation protection professionals. Four fundamental canons: hold paramount public safety, health, and welfare; perform services only in areas of competence; promote advancement of health physics through research, education, practice; conduct respectfully, ethically, and lawfully. Directly relevant to nuclear/radiation physicists.

codes.organization: American Board of Health Physics (ABHP) / American Academy of Health Physics (AAHP)
codes.document_title: Standards of Professional Responsibility for Certified Health Physicists
codes.notes: Certification-based ethical standards for Certified Health Physicists (CHPs). Requires highest standards of professional ethics and integrity. Obligates practice only within areas of competence. Commitment to remain professionally active and knowledgeable of scientific, technical, and regulatory developments. Embedded in ABHP certification requirements.

First produced 1971, substantially revised; current version June 2018. Preamble, six General Principles, and specific Ethical Standards. Covers non-discrimination, research integrity, confidentiality, informed consent, publication ethics, and peer review. Committee on Professional Ethics (COPE) investigates complaints.

codes.document_title: Principles of Professional Responsibility (Statement on Ethics)
codes.notes: First adopted 1971, revised 1998, current version 2012. Seven principles: Do No Harm, Be Open and Honest, Obtain Informed Consent, Weigh Competing Ethical Obligations, Make Results Accessible, Protect and Preserve Records, Maintain Respectful Professional Relationships. Primary obligation to people, species, and materials studied. Notably, AAA does not adjudicate allegations.

Adopted April 20, 2018 after over 200 public comments. Demands honesty, transparency, disinterested assessment, and disclosure of conflicts of interest. Emphasizes equal opportunity regardless of personal attributes. Acceptance required for participation in AEA-sponsored activities. Relatively recent for a major discipline, prompted by profession-wide equity concerns.

codes.document_title: Guide to Professional Ethics in Political Science
codes.notes: First code developed 1967-68 with twenty-one rules of professional conduct. Revised 1989, updated 2022 (Council approved February 2022), updated May 2023. Adopts AAUP Statement on Professional Ethics as baseline. Committee on Professional Ethics, Rights and Freedoms handles grievances and writes guidelines. Includes protections for human subjects research.

Originally issued 1982, significantly revised 2022. Eight sections: Professional Integrity and Accountability, Integrity of Data and Methods, Responsibilities to Stakeholders/Research Subjects/Multidisciplinary Teams/Fellow Practitioners/Profession. 2022 revision notably adds organizational and institutional ethical obligations for the first time. Broad definition of 'statistical practitioner' regardless of job title.

Adopted 1996 by SAA Executive Board, substantially updated March 7, 2024 by member vote. Nine aspirational principles. Aligned with Universal Declaration of Human Rights, UN Declaration on Rights of Indigenous Peoples, and Hague Convention. Emphasizes stewardship, community responsibility, transparency, public engagement, collaboration with Indigenous peoples, and opposition to commercialization.

soc_detailed: 19-3099 Social Scientists and Related Workers, All Other
codes.notes: Approved March 2016. General Principles and Ethical Standards for professional conduct in criminological activities. Distinguishes legal from ethical standards. Emphasizes research integrity, culturally appropriate informed consent, and special protections for vulnerable populations (illiterate, mentally ill, minors). Anonymous reporting via Lighthouse Services hotline.

codes.document_title: Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct
codes.notes: First version 1953, latest revision 2017 with 2024 draft revisions underway. Five aspirational principles (beneficence/nonmaleficence, fidelity/responsibility, integrity, justice, respect for rights/dignity) and ten enforceable standards. Extremely broad applicability across clinical, counseling, school, research, forensic, organizational psychology and more. Violations can lead to membership termination or loss of licensure.

Effective January 1, 2022. Applies to BCaBA and BCBA certificants and applicants. Four core principles: benefit others, treat others with compassion/dignity/respect, behave with integrity, ensure competence. Six standards sections covering professional responsibility, practice, clients/stakeholders, supervisees/trainees, public statements, and research. Notable addition of Standard 1.07 on Cultural Responsiveness and Diversity.

minor_groups.name: Life, Physical, and Social Science Technicians

codes.organization: American Association for Laboratory Animal Science (AALAS)
codes.notes: AALAS certification programs (ALAT, LAT, LATG) for laboratory animal technicians embed ethical requirements for humane and responsible animal care. Founded 1950. Standards integrated into certification rather than published as a standalone code. Applicable to biological and life science technicians working with laboratory animals.

codes.document_title: The Chemical Professional's Code of Conduct
codes.notes: ACS membership and code apply to chemical professionals broadly, including chemical technicians as well as doctoral chemists. Same code listed under 19-2000 (Physical Scientists). Code updated 2019. Covers scientific integrity, professional conduct, responsibility and accountability, and professional development.

minor_groups.name: Occupational Health and Safety Specialists and Technicians

codes.notes: Eight core principles for all BCSP certificants (CSP, ASP, OHST, CHST, STS, CET). Priority: safety and health of individuals and environmental protection. Includes obligations to notify affected parties of unacceptable risk, maintain qualifications, avoid conflicts of interest, and report misconduct. BCSP Judicial Commission can suspend, terminate, or reprimand for violations. Ethics training required for certification maintenance.

Formerly American Society of Safety Engineers (ASSE). Requires service with fidelity, honesty, and impartiality. Obligation to inform appropriate parties of unacceptable risk levels. Professional development through continual improvement. Anti-discrimination provisions. Conflict of interest disclosure requirements. Sets community standards for occupational safety and health professionals.

codes.organization: American Industrial Hygiene Association (AIHA) / American Board of Industrial Hygiene (ABIH) / ACGIH / AAIH
codes.document_title: Code of Ethics for the Professional Practice of Industrial Hygiene
codes.notes: Jointly adopted 1995 by four industrial hygiene organizations: AIHA, ABIH, ACGIH, and AAIH. Protects working people and the public from chemical, microbiological, and physical health hazards. Requires practice following recognized scientific principles. Critical provision: if professional judgment overruled where health and lives are endangered, must notify employer, client, or other authority.

codes.organization: American Board of Health Physics (ABHP) / Health Physics Society (HPS)
codes.notes: For radiation protection professionals who may also serve as occupational health and safety specialists. Four canons: paramount public safety, competence-limited practice, professional advancement, and respectful conduct. Members' duties may directly affect radiation safety of workers and the public. Cross-listed with 19-2000 Physical Scientists.

major_groups.group_name: Life, Physical, and Social Science Occupations

minor_groups.name: Counselors, Social Workers, and Other Community and Social Service Specialists

soc_detailed: 21-1021 Child, Family, and School Social Workers
21-1023 Mental Health and Substance Abuse Social Workers
codes.notes: First adopted 1960, most substantial revision 1996, updated 2017 and 2021. Preamble, six General Principles, and 150+ specific ethical standards across six areas of responsibility. Six core values: service, social justice, dignity and worth of the person, importance of human relationships, integrity, competence. 2021 update added professional self-care language. The definitive code for social work in the US.

codes.organization: International Federation of Social Workers (IFSW) / International Association of Schools of Social Work (IASSW)
codes.document_title: Global Social Work Statement of Ethical Principles
soc_detailed: 21-1021 Child, Family, and School Social Workers
21-1023 Mental Health and Substance Abuse Social Workers
codes.notes: Approved at General Meetings in Dublin, Ireland, July 2018. Replaces 2004 Ethics in Social Work Statement. Principles of social justice, human rights, collective responsibility, and respect for diversities. Addresses digital technology and social media ethical challenges. National associations expected to develop their own codes consistent with this statement.

soc_detailed: 21-1023 Mental Health and Substance Abuse Social Workers
codes.notes: Adopted 1997 by Clinical Social Work Federation, reaffirmed 2006, amended 2016 by CSWA. Supplements (does not replace) the NASW Code of Ethics with focus on clinical social work. Core ethical requirements: non-maleficence, beneficence, and autonomy (client self-determination). Builds upon NASW values of service, social justice, dignity, relationships, integrity, competence.

soc_detailed: 21-1011 Substance Abuse and Behavioral Disorder Counselors
21-1012 Educational, Guidance, and Career Counselors and Advisors
codes.notes: Updated approximately every 10 years; current version 2014. Core principles: autonomy, non-maleficence, beneficence, justice, fidelity, veracity. Covers social media, distance counseling, confidentiality, multiculturalism and diversity, technology use, record keeping, diagnosis, end-of-life care, and prevention of counselor value imposition. Foundational code for the counseling profession.

Revised 2015 and 2020. Six sections focused on clinical mental health counseling practice. Covers commitment to clients, other professionals, students/supervisees/employees, and the public. Addresses confidentiality as a right, integrity and welfare of supervisees, and moral/legal/ethical responsibility to community and public. Ethics Committee continuously reviews and updates.

Updated May 2023, revised August 2023. 114 ethical standards across six areas: professional responsibilities, counseling relationships, supervision/consultation, testing/appraisal/research, counselor education, and telemental health/social media/technology. Applies to all National Certified Counselors (NCCs). Established minimum ethical behaviors for professional certified counselors.

codes.organization: American Association for Marriage and Family Therapy (AAMFT)
codes.notes: First adopted 1962. Revised AAMFT Code of Ethics effective January 1, 2026. Core values include inclusive environment, equity, belonging, mutual respect, diversity/equity/inclusion, systemic and relational therapy excellence, integrity in governance, and innovation. Violations can lead to membership termination, license suspension or revocation. Long history of updates reflecting evolving therapy practice.

codes.organization: International Association of Marriage and Family Counselors (IAMFC)
codes.notes: Published 2017, a division of ACA. Ten sections including The Counseling Relationship and Client Welfare, Assessment and Evaluation, Counselor Education and Supervision, and Diversity and Advocacy. Advocates for family as whole system while considering uniqueness of each member. Emphasizes cultural contexts for couples and families.

codes.document_title: Code of Professional Ethics for Certified Rehabilitation Counselors
codes.notes: First edition 1987, substantial revisions 2002, 2010, 2017, and 2023 (adopted September 2022). Covers counseling relationship, confidentiality, advocacy/accessibility, multicultural considerations, professional responsibility, relationships with other professionals, forensic services, assessment, supervision, research, and technology/social media/virtual counseling. Based partly on ACA Code of Ethics.

codes.organization: NAADAC: The Association for Addiction Professionals / National Certification Commission for Addiction Professionals (NCC AP)
soc_detailed: 21-1011 Substance Abuse and Behavioral Disorder Counselors
codes.notes: Revised 2016, 2021; newest version effective June 1, 2025. Standard of conduct for addiction professionals certified by NCC AP. Covers confidentiality, professional conduct (anti-harassment), public communication (no disparaging persons with substance use disorders), and professional development. Governs counselors working with substance use and addictive behavior disorders.

soc_detailed: 21-1012 Educational, Guidance, and Career Counselors and Advisors
codes.notes: Revised 2015, new 2024 edition released. Over 17,000 words. 2024 updates reflect diverse membership, evolving work settings, and impact of AI on career development. Sets ethical standards including competence-based practice, guidelines for Internet career services, and duty to consult on ethical questions. A division of ACA focused specifically on career development professionals.

codes.document_title: Ethical Standards for Human Services Professionals
soc_detailed: 21-1099 Community and Social Service Specialists, All Other
codes.notes: Revised 2024. Standards of responsibility to seven groups: clients, public and society, colleagues, employers, the profession, self, and students. Protects client right to privacy/confidentiality except where harm may occur. Guides decision-making across broad human services profession. Establishes principles safeguarding client well-being and professional integrity.

codes.organization: American Association of Sexuality Educators, Counselors and Therapists (AASECT)
codes.document_title: AASECT Code of Ethics and Code of Conduct
codes.notes: Revised November 2020. Covers competence and integrity of sex therapists/counselors/educators, confidentiality, welfare of the client, and welfare of students/trainees/research subjects. Ethics Advisory Committee (EAC) promotes ethical conduct through consultation, guidance, education, and misconduct avoidance. Pledge of trust between association and public.

codes.document_title: Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct
codes.notes: Cross-listed from SOC 19-3000 (Psychologists). This code is also directly relevant to clinical and counseling psychologists working in community and social service roles. Five aspirational principles and ten enforceable standards. Standards 4 (Privacy and Confidentiality) and 10 (Therapy) are particularly relevant to community service practice.

codes.organization: Association for Multicultural Counseling and Development (AMCD)
codes.document_title: Multicultural and Social Justice Counseling Competencies
codes.notes: While not a standalone code of ethics, these competencies (endorsed by ACA) function as ethical guidelines for culturally responsive counseling. A division of ACA. Framework addresses counselor self-awareness, client worldview understanding, counseling relationship dynamics, and advocacy at individual, community, and institutional levels.

codes.document_title: Ethical Standards and Code of Conduct
codes.notes: First certification board to establish the specialty profession of Forensic Counselor and Criminal Justice Specialist. Members required to maintain highest professional and ethical standards and represent NAFC to highest standards. Board of Governors includes mental health, criminal justice, addictions, and correctional/law enforcement professionals.

Commitment to accountability for ethical behavior by professional chaplains. Motivated by concern for safety and well-being of members and those served. Recognizes dignity and worth of every individual. Prohibits sexual misconduct, harassment, and assault in client relationships. Takes restorative rather than retributive approach to justice.

codes.organization: Council on Collaboration (APC, ACPE, NACC, NAJC, CAPPE/ACPEP)
codes.document_title: Common Code of Ethics for Chaplains, Pastoral Counselors, Pastoral Educators and Students
codes.notes: Affirmed November 7, 2004 in Portland, Maine by the Council on Collaboration. Unified ethics code for six cognate organizations representing over 10,000 chaplains, pastoral counselors, and clinical pastoral educators. Covers healthcare, counseling centers, prisons, and military settings. Four foundational documents including common standards and principles for processing ethical complaints.

Approved by USCCB subcommittee. Required completion of NACC Ethics Accountability Statement (Code of Ethics 206.11.1) for initial certification and renewal. Addresses breaches of trust: sexual misconduct/harassment, financial misconduct, felonious conduct, misrepresentation of education. Ethics Procedure Manual provides formal complaint processes. Part of BCCI common certification framework.

Embedded in NAJC Bylaws (as amended January 3, 2023). Membership applicants must agree to the Code before membership is granted; renewal indicates continued adherence. Breaches of trust include sexual misconduct/harassment, financial misconduct, felonious conduct, and misrepresentation of education. Sanctions include censure, de-certification, suspension, or expulsion.

Y-2023 revision supersedes all prior provisional codes (1998, 2000, 2001, 2003, 2014). Comprehensive, integrative synthesis of biblical, ethical, legal, clinical, and systemic information. Updates include expanded cultural competency section and new section on technology in counseling. Described as one of the most comprehensive ethics documents in the counseling field.

codes.organization: ACPE: The Standard for Spiritual Care and Education (formerly Association for Clinical Pastoral Education)
codes.document_title: Code of Professional Ethics for Members of ACPE
codes.notes: ACPE is recognized by the U.S. Department of Education as an accrediting agency for clinical pastoral education. Members follow both the ACPE Code and the Common Code of Ethics (2004). Prohibits intentionally false statements about work, requires respect for integrity and welfare of colleagues, and mandates action when concerns about incompetence or misconduct arise. AAPC consolidated with ACPE in 2019.

Adopted by the ABA House of Delegates in 1983, replacing the 1969 Code of Professional Responsibility. Approximately 58 rules organized into eight subject areas: Client-Lawyer Relationship, Counselor, Advocate, Transactions with Persons Other than Clients, Law Firms and Associations, Public Service, Information About Legal Services, and Maintaining the Integrity of the Profession. Adopted with variations in all 50 US states. The foundational ethics code for the American legal profession.

Adopted August 7, 1990; amended 1997, 1999, 2003, 2007, and 2010. Four canons: (1) uphold independence, integrity, and impartiality; (2) perform duties impartially, competently, and diligently; (3) minimize conflicts between personal/extrajudicial activities and judicial obligations; (4) avoid political/campaign activity inconsistent with judicial impartiality. Adopted by most US states as basis for their judicial conduct codes.

codes.document_title: International Principles on Conduct for the Legal Profession
codes.notes: Adopted September 20, 2006; updated 2011 and 2018. Ten core principles developed with input from legal profession representatives across all continents: independence, honesty/integrity/fairness, conflicts of interest, confidentiality, clients' interests, lawyers' undertakings, clients' freedom, property of clients and third parties, competence, and fees. Intended as a universal framework for national codes of conduct.

codes.organization: Council of Bars and Law Societies of Europe (CCBE)
codes.document_title: Code of Conduct for European Lawyers
codes.notes: Adopted 1988, amended multiple times, with Model Code of Conduct for European Lawyers updated 2021. Binding rules governing cross-border legal work within Europe. CCBE represents about one million European lawyers from 32 countries. Accompanied by the Charter of Core Principles of the European Legal Profession (2006), listing ten core principles common to all European bars.

codes.document_title: Basic Principles on the Role of Lawyers
codes.notes: Adopted by the Eighth UN Congress on the Prevention of Crime and the Treatment of Offenders in Havana, 1990. Soft-law instrument defining fundamental requirements for access to independent legal counsel. Key principles: lawyers must not be identified with clients' causes (principle 18); immunity for good-faith professional statements; right to free communication with clients. Landmark international instrument for legal profession independence.

codes.organization: Judicial Group on Strengthening Judicial Integrity / UNODC
codes.notes: Drafted 2001, finalized 2002 at The Hague with participation of International Court of Justice judges. Six core values: Independence, Impartiality, Integrity, Propriety, Equality, Competence and Diligence. Developed in response to concerns about loss of public confidence in the judiciary due to perceptions of corruption. Endorsed by ECOSOC and widely adopted as the international standard for judicial conduct.

codes.document_title: Statement of Good Practices by Law Professors in the Discharge of Their Ethical and Professional Responsibilities
codes.notes: Addresses responsibilities of law professors to students, as scholars, to colleagues, to the law school and university, and to the bar and public. Requires teaching excellence, conscientious exam design, impartial grading, and civil treatment of students. Law professors who are lawyers are also subject to professional ethics of their jurisdiction. Supplements the AAUP Statement on Professional Ethics.

codes.organization: American Arbitration Association (AAA) / American Bar Association (ABA)
codes.document_title: Code of Ethics for Arbitrators in Commercial Disputes
codes.notes: Originally prepared 1977 by joint ABA-AAA committee; revised 2003 by ABA Task Force and AAA special committee. Applies to commercial arbitration but not labor arbitration (which uses the separate Code of Professional Responsibility for Arbitrators of Labor-Management Disputes). 2004 revision applies a presumption of neutrality to all arbitrators, including party-appointed ones. Covers disclosure, impartiality, conflicts of interest, and communication.

codes.organization: American Bar Association (ABA) / American Arbitration Association (AAA) / Association for Conflict Resolution (ACR)
codes.document_title: Model Standards of Conduct for Mediators
codes.notes: Originally prepared 1994 by joint ABA/AAA/ACR committee; revised 2005 and approved by all three organizations. Nine standards: self-determination, impartiality, conflicts of interest, competence, confidentiality, quality of the process, advertising/solicitation, fees, and advancement of mediation practice. Fundamental ethical guidelines for mediators in all practice contexts.

First adopted 1991; revised 2010 as Code of Professional Responsibility; further revised March 2021. Covers ethical administration of private firms, legal clinics, corporate legal departments, governmental agencies, and courts. Requires compatibility with ABA Model Rules of Professional Conduct, continuing education, protection of confidential information, and promotion of diversity and inclusion in legal management.

codes.document_title: Notary Public Code of Professional Responsibility
codes.notes: First-ever detailed code of ethical and professional conduct for notaries, updated in 2020 edition. Guiding principles include impartiality, identity verification, confidentiality, record-keeping, and continuous education on notarization laws. The notary shall act as an impartial witness and not profit from any document or transaction apart from the fee allowed by statute.

Adopted 1970, recently updated 2023 when NALI Executive Council adopted 'Code of Professional Conduct: Standards and Ethics for the Investigative Profession, 4th ed.' as highest standard. Investigator must be dedicated to search for truth, maintain proper licensing, conduct investigations with integrity and honesty, respect rights of all persons, and accurately represent services. Certified Legal Investigators (CLI) must adhere to this code.

Guide for title companies and employees in the title insurance industry. Key principles: engage only in lawful business practices consistent with high ethical standards; encourage culture of compliance with federal and state laws; treat consumers fairly and ethically; provide timely and comprehensive information regarding policies, services, products, and prices; and educate consumers about title insurance. ALTA founded 1907, representing 6,000+ title insurance agents and abstracters.

Aspirational principles adopted April 5, 1999. Promote open, equitable, and effective access to legal information; protect patron confidentiality, privacy, and personal data; recognize duty to avoid unauthorized practice of law; promote fair and ethical trade practices; do not allow personal convictions to lead to inequitable service. AALL also endorses the ALA Code of Ethics.

codes.document_title: NALA Code of Ethics and Professional Responsibility
codes.notes: Canons covering the paralegal profession. Key provisions: Canon 1 prohibits unauthorized practice of law, establishing attorney-client relationships, and giving legal opinions; Canon 3 permits tasks properly delegated and supervised by attorneys; Canon 6 requires integrity and competency through continuing education; Canon 7 protects client confidences and privileged communications; Canon 8 requires disclosure of conflicts of interest. Revised March 2022.

codes.document_title: Model Code of Ethics and Professional Responsibility
codes.notes: Adopted May 1993 as aspirational guide; made enforceable April 1997 with adoption of Model Disciplinary Rules. Covers competence (education, training, continuing education), billing accuracy, prohibition of ex parte communications with courts, professional title disclosure, and confidentiality. Expresses NFPA's commitment to increasing quality and efficiency of legal services.

codes.organization: NALS — National Association for Legal Support Professionals
codes.document_title: NALS Code of Ethics and Professional Responsibility
codes.notes: Seven canons governing paralegals, legal assistants, legal secretaries, and all legal services professionals. Canon 1: maintain competency and integrity through continuing education; Canon 2: maintain ethical conduct and association integrity; Canon 3: avoid conflicts of interest; Canon 4: preserve client confidences and privileged communications; Canon 6: shall not solicit legal business on behalf of a lawyer; Canon 7: shall not perform paralegal functions except under direct lawyer supervision (unless permitted by law).

Mandatory code defining ethical relationships between court reporters and the public, bench, and bar. Requirements: be fair and impartial toward each participant; disclose actual or potential conflicts of interest; guard against appearance of impropriety; preserve confidentiality and security of information; be truthful in public statements about qualifications. Accompanied by Guidelines for Professional Practice (aspirational goals). Overseen by the Committee on Professional Ethics (COPE), which has issued 44+ advisory opinions.

Adopted April 1966, revised 1987 and 2009. Addresses five areas of responsibility: as teachers (encourage free pursuit of learning, respect students as individuals, ensure evaluations reflect true merit), as scholars (seek and state truth), as colleagues (respect colleagues, do not discriminate or harass), as members of institutions, and as citizens (promote conditions of free inquiry). Foundational document for academic ethics.

codes.organization: NASPA — Student Affairs Administrators in Higher Education
codes.document_title: NASPA Guiding Principles and Code of Ethics
codes.notes: Adapted from Higher Education Consortium for Student Affairs Certification Code of Ethics. Three-part structure: guiding principles (overall objectives), aspirational goals, and ethical obligations. Eight guiding principles: integrity and honesty, confidentiality and privacy, quality and excellence, continuous learning, inclusivity and equity, respect for diversity, well-being, and dignity/respect/compassion.

codes.organization: Council for the Advancement of Standards in Higher Education (CAS)
codes.document_title: CAS Statement of Shared Ethical Principles
codes.notes: Seven shared ethical principles: autonomy, non-malfeasance, beneficence, justice, fidelity, veracity, and affiliation. CAS represents 42 higher education and student affairs professional organizations. Not intended to replace individual association codes but articulates shared foundational principles across student services professions. CAS established 1979.

codes.organization: International Association of Universities (IAU) / Magna Charta Observatory (MCO)
codes.document_title: IAU-MCO Guidelines for an Institutional Code of Ethics in Higher Education
codes.notes: Approved at 14th IAU General Conference 2012. Provides comprehensive guidelines for universities to develop or review institutional codes of ethics. Developed after 2010 IAU International Conference on Values and Ethics in Vilnius.

Guidelines for TESOL members, volunteers, and participants. Requires members to embrace TESOL's mission and commitment to diversity, equity, inclusion, and access; uphold the profession's reputation through respectful actions; encourage and support colleagues in professional development; and act with integrity and respect. TESOL teacher preparation standards also include professional ethics requirements emphasizing truth, democratic citizenship, and human dignity.

minor_groups.name: Preschool, Elementary, Middle, Secondary, and Special Education Teachers

codes.notes: Adopted 1975 by the nation's largest professional employee organization (3 million members). Two core principles: Commitment to the Student (non-discrimination, academic freedom, confidentiality, protection from harmful conditions, fair evaluation) and Commitment to the Profession (honest representation of qualifications, prohibitions on misrepresentation, protecting colleagues). Foundational code for American public education.

Adopted by AFT Executive Council October 3, 2018; updated July 2023. Governs member conduct and organizational representation. Members must serve all members equitably without prejudice and comport themselves in ways not detrimental to the organization's reputation. AFT also endorsed the MCEE and developed a separate Code of Ethical International Recruitment and Employment of Teachers.

codes.organization: National Association for the Education of Young Children (NAEYC)
codes.document_title: Code of Ethical Conduct and Statement of Commitment
codes.notes: Adopted 1989, updated 2005, reaffirmed 2011, with current revision in draft as of 2024. Four sections: relationships with children, families, colleagues, and community/society. Applies to all individuals caring for children birth through age 8. Offers guidelines for responsible behavior and a common basis for resolving principal ethical dilemmas in early childhood care and education.

codes.organization: National Association of State Directors of Teacher Education and Certification (NASDTEC)
codes.document_title: Model Code of Ethics for Educators (MCEE)
codes.notes: 2nd edition July 2023. Five principles: responsibility to the profession, professional competence, responsibility to students, responsibility to the school community, responsible and ethical use of technology. Developed collaboratively with NEA, AFT, and other organizations. Overseen by the National Council for the Advancement of Educator Ethics (NCAEE), established 2015 to promote ethical decision-making that impacts the safety and well-being of children.

codes.document_title: ASCA Ethical Standards for School Counselors
codes.notes: Developed collaboratively with practitioners and counselor educators nationwide. Covers Pre-K through 12. Sections: Responsibility to Students, Parents/Guardians, School Staff, Self, Administrators/Supervisors, Intern Site Supervisors, Maintenance of Standards, and Ethical Decision Making. Revised 2010, 2016, and 2022. 2022 update expands language about school counselors as leaders, advocates, collaborators, and consultants who create systemic change.

International ethics declaration for teachers and education personnel worldwide. Six articles: Commitment to the Profession, Commitment to Students, Commitment to Colleagues, Commitment to Management Personnel, Commitment to Parents, Commitment to the Teacher. Education International is the global hub for teacher unions representing 32.5 million education employees from 383 organizations in 178 countries. Designed to create professional identity and unity among teachers globally.

codes.document_title: Recommendation concerning the Status of Teachers
codes.notes: Adopted October 5, 1966 at special intergovernmental conference convened by UNESCO in Paris. Sets forth rights and responsibilities of teachers, international standards for preparation, recruitment, employment, and teaching conditions. Specifically recommends that codes of ethics be established by teachers' organizations to ensure professional prestige. Non-binding recommendation for all ILO/UNESCO member states. Complemented by 1997 UNESCO Recommendation on Higher-Education Teaching Personnel.

Ethical principles for tutors: guide students to do their own work; maintain professional (not personal) relationships; be punctual; keep student information confidential; provide honest feedback via positive praise and constructive suggestions; respect cultural backgrounds and personal value systems; keep current in subject areas and learning methodologies. NTA also has a separate Academic Coach Code of Ethics. Dedicated to achieving and maintaining high professional standards for tutors and tutoring programs.

codes.document_title: Standards for Initial TESOL Pre-K-12 Teacher Preparation Programs
codes.notes: Professional teaching standards with embedded ethics requirements for ESL/EFL instructors. Candidates should strive toward excellence, recognize the importance of truth, nurture democratic citizenship, safeguard freedom to learn and teach, and believe in human dignity and educational opportunities for all. Includes the 6 Principles for Exemplary Teaching of English Learners drawn from decades of language pedagogy research.

Created 1939, most recently amended 2021 with addition of ninth principle on racial and social justice, diversity, equity, and inclusion. Nine core principles addressing intellectual freedom, privacy and confidentiality, resistance to censorship, fair representation of all viewpoints, equitable access, and professional excellence. Framework for ethical decision-making used by librarians, library staff, and information professionals. Complemented by the Library Bill of Rights.

codes.organization: International Federation of Library Associations and Institutions (IFLA)
codes.document_title: IFLA Code of Ethics for Librarians and Other Information Workers
codes.notes: Approved and endorsed August 2012 by IFLA's Committee on Freedom of Access to Information and Freedom of Expression (FAIFE). Covers access to information (rejecting censorship by states, governments, or institutions), free access to collections, professional conduct, copyright balance, and privacy. Translated into multiple languages for worldwide use. Serves as model and reference for national library association codes.

Guidelines positioned within interacting value systems: basic human rights, organizational missions, legal/cultural/societal norms, and personal ethical beliefs. Core principles: integrity, competence, diligence, honesty, discretion, confidentiality, accurate self-representation, avoidance of conflicts of interest. Recognizes different types of information (personally identifiable, proprietary, classified, public) and respects diversity of viewpoints and cultural differences.

codes.organization: Association of College and Research Libraries (ACRL/ALA)
codes.document_title: Code of Ethics for Special Collections Librarians
codes.notes: First appeared as 'Standards for Ethical Conduct for Rare Book, Manuscript, and Special Collections Librarians' in 1987; second edition 1993; recast as Code of Ethics with commentary 2003; current version approved June 19, 2020 by ACRL Board. Practitioners must be familiar with and adhere to the ALA Code of Ethics. Addresses unique ethical issues in special collections including personal collecting, appraisal, donor relations, and access restrictions.

Aspirational principles for law librarians adopted April 5, 1999. Promote open, equitable access to legal information; protect patron confidentiality, privacy, and personal data; recognize duty to avoid unauthorized practice of law; promote fair trade practices; do not allow personal convictions to lead to inequitable service. AALL also endorses the ALA Code of Ethics. Bridges both legal and library professional ethics obligations.

codes.document_title: SAA Core Values Statement and Code of Ethics
codes.notes: First introduced 1980, updated 1992, significantly revised August 2020. Provides ethical framework addressing professional relationships, authentic records, physical protection of materials, access, privacy protection for donors and users. Goal: move the profession toward a more inclusive, ethical, and accountable community of archival practice. Must be read in conjunction with SAA's Core Values of Archivists.

Adopted September 6, 1996 at ICA General Assembly in Beijing. Available in 24 languages. Key principles: protect integrity of archival material as reliable evidence; perform duties in accordance with archival principles regarding creation, maintenance, selection, preservation, and description of records; promote widest possible access while respecting privacy and acting within relevant legislation. Term 'archivists' encompasses all concerned with control, care, and preservation of archives.

Adopted November 12, 1993 by AAM Board of Directors; revised 2000. Five sections plus afterword covering Governance, Collections, Programs, and Promulgation. Root value: commitment to serving present and future generations. Loyalty to mission and public must never be compromised by conflicts of interest. Museums must act not only legally but ethically, frequently exceeding legal minimums. AAM recommends each member museum adopt its own institutional code applying these principles.

codes.document_title: ICOM Code of Ethics for Museums
codes.notes: First adopted 1986, revised 2004, translated into 38 languages. Sets minimum professional standards and promotes shared values for the international museum community. Covers acquisition procedures, legislation compliance, resource management, security, returns and restitutions, and due diligence/provenance (key role in fighting illicit traffic). Currently undergoing fourth consultation for revision, with vote expected at ICOM Annual Meeting June 2026.

codes.organization: Association of Registrars and Collections Specialists (ARCS) / Collections Stewardship of AAM (CS-AAM)
codes.document_title: Code of Ethics and Professional Practices for Collections Professionals
codes.notes: Originally authored 1984 as 'Code of Ethics for Registrars' (first to address ethical issues specific to collections management and registration); revised 2021 by joint CS-AAM/ARCS task force. Part of AAM's Framework for Museum Excellence. Covers ethical management of collections held in public trust, including acquisition, deaccessioning, loans, insurance, and documentation. Both ARCS and AAM endorsed the updated version.

Based on ANA Center for Ethics and Human Rights. Core values: child well-being, diversity/equity/inclusion, excellence, innovation, integrity, leadership, scholarship. Updated 2024. Covers school nursing practice including advocacy, dignity, equity, and competency. Included in this group because school nurses work within educational settings under SOC 25-9000.

minor_groups.name: Other Educational Instruction and Library Occupations

codes.notes: First adopted 1974; revised 1984, 1992, 1997, 2000, and 2020.
