Four themes: respecting dignity and rights, professional competence, honesty and integrity, and responsibility to schools/families/communities/profession/society. 17 ethical principles. Effective July 2020 revision. Covers school psychology practice across PreK-12 settings.

codes.document_title: Recommendation on Education for Peace, Human Rights and Sustainable Development
codes.notes: Adopted November 2023 by UNESCO's 194 Member States. 14 guiding principles including ethic of care, compassion, solidarity, and global citizenship. Non-binding guidance for reshaping education systems. Replaces 1974 Recommendation. Addresses ethical frameworks for educational workers broadly across all instructional contexts.

Ethical principles for professionals in international education and exchange. Covers integrity, truthfulness, competence, service orientation, cultural sensitivity, respect for diversity, and advocacy for international students and scholars. NAFSA serves international educators, advisors, and administrators across higher education and related settings.

codes.document_title: NTA Academic Coach Code of Ethics
codes.notes: Separate code for academic coaches (distinct from the tutor code). Dedicated to providing members with opportunities to achieve and maintain high professional standards for academic coaches and administrators of academic coaching programs. Covers professional conduct, student-centered learning, confidentiality, cultural sensitivity, and continuous professional development.

codes.organization: AIGA — the Professional Association for Design
codes.notes: Standards organized by responsibilities: to clients, to other designers, to the public, and to society and the environment. Encourages designers to contribute 5% of time to public-good projects. Addresses confidentiality, fair competition, intellectual property, and environmental responsibility.

codes.document_title: Code of Fair Practice for the Graphic Communications Industry
codes.notes: Revised 1989; originally formulated in the 1940s. Promotes equity for those creating, selling, buying, and using graphic works. Addresses credit attribution, prohibition of plagiarism, portfolio handling, fair remuneration, and artists' right to sign work. Companion document: Graphic Artists Guild Handbook: Pricing & Ethical Guidelines (17th edition).

codes.document_title: ICoD Code of Professional Conduct for Designers
codes.notes: International framework for professional conduct for graphic designers. Published through the Graphic Artists Guild as 'Doing Good Work: A Professional Code of Conduct for Graphic Artists.' Covers professional competence, integrity, confidentiality, and social responsibility.

minor_groups.name: Entertainers and Performers, Sports and Related Workers

codes.organization: SAG-AFTRA (Screen Actors Guild–American Federation of Television and Radio Artists)
codes.notes: Addresses workplace behavior, sexual harassment prevention, and professional standards for performers. Part of SAG-AFTRA's Four Pillars of Change Initiative. Members expected to uphold standards in dealings with other members and employees.

codes.document_title: Personal Manager Code of Ethics and Conduct
codes.notes: First-ever personal manager code. Voluntary agreement promoting honest and ethical relationships between members and their managers. Requires managers to put member interests first, act honestly, not solicit employment except under franchised agent direction. Includes arbitration for dispute resolution.

codes.document_title: PGA Member Policies and Code of Conduct
codes.notes: Emphasizes integrity, honesty, and professionalism in production. Addresses fair treatment of cast and crew, responsible budgeting, and compliance with industry regulations. PGA operates with Hollywood Commission in unified framework sharing Code of Conduct and policy templates. Updated January 2025.

Voluntary guidelines for directors and executives who work with directors, developed by the DGA-Employers Creative Rights Committee. Covers preparation time, creative control, director's cut rights, notes and feedback processes, and key personnel selection.

codes.document_title: WGA Community Standards and Code of Working Rules
codes.notes: Community standards requiring professional conduct in all work settings (writers' rooms, sets, meetings). Code of Working Rules prohibits accepting misrepresented credits, working on speculation, and mandates reporting employment as producer/director. Addresses harassment, discrimination, and power dynamics.

Original code borrowed from ASNE 1926; SPJ wrote its own 1973, revised 1984, 1987, 1996, 2014. Four core principles: seek truth and report it, minimize harm, act independently, be accountable and transparent. Voluntary and not legally enforceable under the First Amendment. Foundational document for American journalism ethics.

Most recently revised June 2015. Emphasizes accuracy, fairness, transparency, and accountability. Addresses minimizing harm to vulnerable individuals. Accompanied by detailed coverage guidelines for common and uncommon ethical situations prepared by journalists, managers, and subject-area experts.

codes.document_title: IFJ Global Charter of Ethics for Journalists
codes.notes: Adopted at the 30th IFJ World Congress in Tunis, June 2019, by 300 delegates from 100+ countries. Completes the 1954 IFJ Declaration of Principles on the Conduct of Journalists (Bordeaux Declaration). 16 articles plus preamble. Based on the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Defines duties and rights regarding ethics for journalists globally.

codes.document_title: NPPA Code of Ethics for Visual Journalists
codes.notes: Founded 1946. Promotes highest standards in visual journalism. Prohibits altering photographic content electronically or in the darkroom in ways that deceive the public. Standards include accuracy, avoiding manipulation, respecting subjects' dignity, special consideration for vulnerable subjects, and avoiding staging or altering scenes.

First developed 1950; current version has preamble, statement of professional values, and six code provisions. Six core values: advocacy, honesty, expertise, independence, loyalty, fairness. Membership may be restricted for violations. Widely regarded as the cornerstone ethical code for public relations practice.

codes.document_title: AAF Advertising Principles of American Business
codes.notes: Principles emphasizing truthfulness in advertising, substantiation of claims, non-deceptive practices, and respect for all audience segments. Addresses privacy, discrimination, endorsements transparency, and distinguishing ads from editorial/news content. Compliance is voluntary but widely recognized as industry best practice.

codes.document_title: IABC Code of Ethics for Professional Communicators
codes.notes: Based on three principles: professional communication is legal, ethical, and in good taste. Addresses honesty, accuracy, correcting misinformation, not engaging in practices that corrupt channels of communication, and protecting confidential information.

Originally adopted 1975 as ASNE Statement of Principles. Addresses responsibility, freedom of the press, independence, truth and accuracy, impartiality, and fair play. The oldest journalism ethics code in the U.S. was the ASNE Canons of Journalism (1923) which this document succeeded.

Founded 1964. Establishes principles of honesty, justice, and courtesy for broadcast engineers. Emphasizes integrity as keystone of professional conduct. Covers fidelity to public and employers, impartiality, dignity of profession, confidentiality, avoidance of conflicts of interest, professional development, and information sharing.

major_groups.group_name: Arts, Design, Entertainment, Sports, and Media Occupations

codes.notes: First adopted 1847; continuously updated. Nine Principles of Medical Ethics plus Council on Ethical and Judicial Affairs Opinions organized by chapter. Covers patient-physician relationships, consent, privacy, genetics, organ transplantation, research, and more. The most comprehensive and authoritative professional medical ethics code in the U.S.

Nine aspirational principles adopted 1957, revised 1980, 2001. Separate from the full Code. Defines honorable behavior: competence, honesty, respect for law, continuing education, community service, freedom to choose patients.

codes.document_title: WMA International Code of Medical Ethics
codes.notes: First adopted 1949 as complement to the Declaration of Geneva. Major 2022 revision (4-year process) adds provisions on environmental health, remote care, physician well-being. Defines professional duties toward patients, other physicians, health professionals, themselves, and society worldwide.

codes.document_title: WMA Declaration of Geneva — The Physician's Pledge
codes.notes: Modern Hippocratic Oath; first adopted 1948. 2017 revision was the largest in decades, adding patient autonomy, physician self-care, medical knowledge sharing. Amended 1948, 1968, 1983, 1994, editorially revised 2005, 2006, amended 2017.

Applies to all osteopathic physicians from enrollment through practice. Addresses confidentiality, candid communication with patients, physician-patient trust, community responsibility, and research standards. Transcends economic, political, and religious biases.

codes.document_title: Code of Ethics for Nurses with Interpretive Statements
codes.notes: First formally adopted 1950. 2025 revision (over 6,000 nurses consulted, 49-expert panel, 600+ hours): retains 9 provisions with edits, adds new 10th provision affirming nursing's role in advancing human and environmental well-being worldwide. Addresses health disparities, racism, allyship, workplace safety, and emerging technologies.

codes.document_title: ICN Code of Ethics for Nurses
codes.notes: First adopted 1953, revised 1965, 1973 (new code), reaffirmed 1989, revised 2000, 2012, 2021. Four elements: nurses and people, nurses and practice, nurses and coworkers, nurses and the profession. Emphasizes advocacy for human rights of patients, families, and communities.

codes.document_title: ADA Principles of Ethics and Code of Professional Conduct
codes.notes: Three components: Principles of Ethics (aspirational), Code of Professional Conduct (enforceable rules), Advisory Opinions. Five fundamental principles: patient autonomy, nonmaleficence, beneficence, justice, veracity. Binding on ADA members; violations may result in discipline. Updated continuously.

codes.document_title: International Principles of Ethics for the Dental Profession
codes.notes: Guidelines for every dentist and dental team member. Covers practicing according to science and principles of humanity, safeguarding oral health irrespective of patient status, referral obligations, continuing education duties, and public oral health education. Companion: FDI Dental Ethics Manual (2nd edition).

Established 1852, most recently revised 1994. Eight principles covering covenantal patient-pharmacist relationship, patient care, autonomy, dignity, justice, competence, individual and community health, and professional obligations. Endorsed by ASHP (1996) and AMCP.

codes.document_title: FIP Statement of Professional Standards — Code of Ethics for Pharmacists
codes.notes: Approved by FIP Council 2014; builds on 1988 guidelines and 1997 statement. Deliberately broad framework for nations to adapt. Centers on autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice. Covers independence of profession, refusal to dispense when serving patient health, pharmacists as health educators, and patient freedom of choice.

codes.document_title: Code of Ethics for the Physical Therapy Profession
codes.notes: Adopted July 2025 by APTA House of Delegates, effective January 2026. Combines former Code of Ethics for PT with Standards of Ethical Conduct for PTA into one document. Core values: accountability, altruism, collaboration, compassion, duty, excellence, integrity, social responsibility. Enforceable through Ethics and Judicial Committee.

codes.document_title: AOTA 2025 Occupational Therapy Code of Ethics
codes.notes: First established 1975; reviewed every 5 years. 2025 revision reflects evolving healthcare landscape and emerging technologies. Seven core values: altruism, equality, freedom, justice, dignity, truth, prudence. Some states use AOTA Code as part of licensure acts.

First formalized 1952 for audiologists and speech-language pathologists. Partly obligatory and disciplinary, partly aspirational. Enforced by Board of Ethics with confidential administration. At least 1 hour of ethics CE required per 3-year certification cycle. Covers 247,000+ members and affiliates.

codes.document_title: Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct
codes.notes: Current version adopted 2002, amended 2010, 2017. Five aspirational principles: beneficence/nonmaleficence, fidelity/responsibility, integrity, justice, respect for rights/dignity. Ten enforceable standards covering competence, human relations, privacy, advertising, record keeping, education, research, assessment, therapy. Violations can result in license loss.

codes.document_title: Principles of Medical Ethics with Annotations Especially Applicable to Psychiatry
codes.notes: First published 1973. Adopts AMA Principles with psychiatry-specific annotations. Includes the famous Goldwater Rule (Section 7.3) prohibiting public commentary on non-examined individuals' mental health. Membership condition; violations can lead to reprimand, suspension, or expulsion.

codes.document_title: AOA Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct
codes.notes: Standards of Professional Conduct adopted June 2011. Guided by four bioethical principles: patient autonomy, non-maleficence, beneficence, justice. Core duties: patient health paramount, respect dignity, advise on referrals, maintain confidentiality, ensure access, advance competence, maintain professional standards. Accompanied by Optometric Oath.

Thirteen principles covering professional excellence, professional conduct, doctor-patient relationships, patient confidentiality, professional accountability, community service, and reporting of unethical acts. Adherence required for ACA membership. Primary responsibility is patient benefit.

Founded 1912. Members obligated to follow code. Covers patient safety, appropriate supervision, prohibition of referral kickbacks in federal programs. Approximately 80% of U.S. podiatrists are members.

Comprises Principles, Code of Conduct, and Definitions. Three fundamental principles: stewardship, integrity, respect. Code of Conduct covers delivering competent care, balancing patient welfare with client needs and public safety, and maintaining professionalism. Revised 2015 and updated 2024 draft. Enforceable through state veterinary boards.

Initially published 1974, revised March 2004, updated April 2016. Describes Code of Professional Conduct, Qualifications of Surgeons, and surgeon-patient relationship. Covers qualifications, patient relations, interprofessional relations, medical education, and surgeons and society. Reviewed by Board of Regents.

codes.document_title: Guidelines for the Ethical Practice of Anesthesiology
codes.notes: Originally approved October 2003, last amended October 2025. Recognizes AMA Principles as basic guide. Five areas of ethical responsibility: to patients, to medical colleagues, to health care facilities, to themselves, and to community/society. Emphasizes patient self-determination and informed consent.

codes.organization: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG)
codes.document_title: Code of Professional Ethics of ACOG
codes.notes: Sections on ethical foundations, physician conduct and practice, conflicts of interest, professional relations, and societal responsibilities. Addresses problems unique to women's health. Patient welfare as basis of all medical judgments. Noncompliance may affect Fellowship status.

codes.document_title: Code of Ethics for Emergency Physicians
codes.notes: Approved 1997; revised 2008, 2016, 2017, October 2023. Recognizes unique nature of emergency care and moral challenges. Covers beneficence, non-maleficence, autonomy, justice, and impartial treatment. Enforceable with formal review process for violations.

Three-part structure: Principles of Ethics (aspirational), Rules of Ethics (mandatory/enforceable), Administrative Procedures. Enforced by Ethics Committee and Board of Trustees. Penalties: admonition, censure, suspension, or termination of membership. Best interest of patient as guiding principle.

codes.document_title: Guidelines for Ethical Conduct for the PA Profession
codes.notes: Current code adopted 1983, amended 1985, reaffirmed 1990. Upholds patient autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice. Covers professional conduct, confidentiality, community service, sexual conduct prohibitions, harassment/discrimination, and research honesty.

codes.document_title: ACNM Code of Ethics with Explanatory Statements
codes.notes: Describes moral obligations guiding midwife behaviors. Foundation: respect for basic human rights and dignity of all persons. Emphasizes confidentiality, accountability, advocacy for women's rights in healthcare. Developed alongside Standards for the Practice of Midwifery and ACNM Philosophy.

codes.document_title: ICM International Code of Ethics for Midwives
codes.notes: Four sections: midwifery relationships, practice of midwifery, professional responsibilities, advancement of knowledge/practice. Based on recognition of women's human rights, mutual respect, trust, dignity. Covers informed decision-making, evidence-based practice, confidentiality, and right to privacy.

Last amended November 2017. Covers professional relationships with colleagues, patients, organization members, community, and society. Requires honesty, integrity, equity, fairness. Mandates patient care above other considerations, resource allocation with ethical transparency. Membership requirement.

codes.organization: Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics / Commission on Dietetic Registration (CDR)
codes.document_title: Code of Ethics for the Nutrition and Dietetics Profession
codes.notes: Effective June 2018. Applies to RDNs and NDTRs. Core values: customer focus, integrity, innovation, social responsibility, diversity. Updated to address digital health care, social media, and evolving technologies. Principles: honesty/integrity, high professional standards, public health/safety/welfare.

codes.document_title: AARC Statement of Ethics and Professional Conduct
codes.notes: Effective April 2015. Covers integrity, objectivity, trust, competence, respect for patient rights (privacy, informed consent, refusal of treatment), non-discrimination, avoidance of fraud and conflicts of interest, and promoting access and cost-effective care.

codes.organization: National Association of Emergency Medical Technicians (NAEMT)
codes.notes: Originally written by Charles B. Gillespie, M.D., adopted 1978, revised June 2013. Pledges to conserve life, alleviate suffering, promote health, do no harm, encourage equal availability of care. 2013 revision updates terminology and adds non-discrimination regarding socioeconomic status. Core: compassion, accountability, integrity.

codes.document_title: Code of Ethics for EMS Physician Medical Directors
codes.notes: Jointly adopted by NAEMSP, NASEMSO, and AMPA. Establishes principles of honorable behavior for EMS medical directors recognizing responsibility to public, EMS practitioners, and health care systems. Published in Prehospital Emergency Care journal.

codes.document_title: AAMA Code of Ethics and Medical Assisting Creed
codes.notes: Code covers dignity of humanity, confidentiality, honor of profession, and continuous knowledge/skill improvement. Companion Creed affirms dedication to patient care and well-being, loyalty to employer, and commitment to professional principles. Medical assistants also adhere to separate Creed statement.

Formalized 1993; updated 2020, 2023, 2025. Two parts: Code of Ethics (aspirational, 11 principles) and Rules of Ethics (mandatory, enforceable). Certificate holders must notify ARRT of ethics violations including state licensing issues and criminal charges within 30 days.

Jointly developed with ARRT. Principles cover professional manner, respect for patient dignity, service without discrimination, patient confidentiality, continuous improvement of knowledge/skills, and evidence-based practice. Expected of every ASRT member and ARRT registrant.

codes.organization: American Society for Clinical Laboratory Science (ASCLS)
codes.notes: Three concentric-circle duties: duty to patient (center), duty to colleagues and profession, duty to society. Patient welfare above own needs; high-quality care that is safe, effective, efficient, timely, equitable, patient-centered. Includes patient advocacy and equitable healthcare resource distribution.

Established by AMT Board of Directors. Defines competent, honorable, and ethical behavior for AMT-certified professionals. Covers avoiding dishonest/unethical/illegal practices, patient welfare above all, respecting patient rights, safeguarding confidences. Required for certification maintenance.

codes.organization: Nuclear Medicine Technology Certification Board (NMTCB) / Society of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging (SNMMI)
codes.document_title: Code of Ethics for Nuclear Medicine Technologists
codes.notes: Adopted at 2004 SNMMI Annual Meeting. Seven principles: compassion and respect for dignity, non-discrimination, strict patient confidentiality per federal/state regulations, compliance with laws, continual skill improvement, no fraud/deception/criminal activity, and professional advocacy.

Applies to all AHIMA members, CCHIIM certification holders, and students. Core principles: advocate patient privacy/confidentiality, service before self-interest, protect sensitive information (genetic, adoption, substance use, sexual health, behavioral), truthful credentials, interdisciplinary collaboration. Enforceable and aspirational elements.

Revised May 2022. Five shared professional values: caring/compassion, integrity, respect, competence, accountability. Covers equitable treatment, regulatory compliance, positive representation of profession, ethical conduct including appropriate relationships, and patient safety/advocacy.

codes.organization: National Certification Commission for Acupuncture and Oriental Medicine (NCCAOM)
codes.notes: NCCAOM establishes, assesses, and promotes recognized standards of competence and safety in acupuncture and Oriental medicine. Code covers patient safety, professional integrity, informed consent, scope of practice, non-discrimination, and continuing education requirements.

minor_groups.name: Other Healthcare Practitioners and Technical Occupations

codes.document_title: AAP Code of Conduct and Bioethics Committee Policy Statements
codes.notes: Committee on Bioethics began 1979 (ad hoc), official AAP committee 1985. Section on Bioethics founded 1988. Writes policy statements on bioethical issues in pediatrics: consent/decision-making for minors, confidentiality, end-of-life care, research involving children, resource allocation. Guided by beneficence, non-maleficence, autonomy, justice.

codes.document_title: AAFP Ethics and AMA Principles of Medical Ethics Policy
codes.notes: AAFP references AMA Principles of Medical Ethics as foundational ethics policy. Additionally provides Curriculum Guideline on Medical Ethics covering clinical, professional, and medico-legal topics, and separate guidelines for ethical participation in research. 128,300+ members.

codes.organization: World Health Organization (WHO) / World Federation for Medical Education (WFME)
codes.document_title: WFME Global Standards for Quality Improvement of Medical Education
codes.notes: Third edition 2020. Promotes highest scientific and ethical standards in medical education globally. Covers basic medical education, postgraduate education, and continuing professional development. Encourages integrated programs in biomedical, clinical, behavioral, and social sciences including medical ethics. Principles-based approach for local adaptation.

minor_groups.name: Home Health and Personal Care Aides; Nursing Assistants, Orderlies, and Psychiatric Aides

codes.organization: National Association of Health Care Assistants (NAHCA)
codes.document_title: CNA Code of Ethics and Federal Regulations Handbook
codes.notes: Founded 1995 by former CNAs Lori Porter and Lisa Sweet. NAHCA is the only national association exclusively for Certified Nursing Assistants. The CNA Code of Ethics and Federal Regulations Handbook educates members on ethical conduct and performance standards. Members take an oath of service committing to ethical practice and leadership. Core values include preserving life, easing suffering, restoring health, dignity, and teamwork.

codes.organization: National Alliance for Direct Support Professionals (NADSP)
codes.document_title: NADSP Code of Ethics for Direct Support Professionals
occupations_covered: 31-1120 Home Health and Personal Care Aides
codes.notes: Developed in 2000 by a national panel including DSPs, self-advocates, family members, and researchers. Nine areas of ethical conduct: person-centered supports, promoting physical and emotional well-being, integrity and responsibility, confidentiality, justice/fairness/equity, respect, self-determination, relationships, and advocacy. First allegiance is to the person supported. Widely adopted by state agencies (e.g., New York OPWDD mandates it). Accompanied by DSP Dialogues training manual.

codes.organization: National Association for Home Care & Hospice (NAHC) / National Alliance for Care at Home
occupations_covered: 31-1120 Home Health and Personal Care Aides
codes.notes: Adopted 1982. Eight sections covering: patient rights and responsibilities, services to patients/families, fair billing and pricing, marketing and representation, relationships with other providers, personnel management, compliance with laws and regulations, and community responsibility. Ethics Committee of at least three disinterested parties handles breach complaints; may suspend or expel members. NAHC rebranded to National Alliance for Care at Home.

Adopted September 18, 1996, by the California Association of Psychiatric Technicians. Code accompanied by Interpretive Statements that expand on each item. Framework for ethical decisions regarding responsibilities to clients/patients, public, interdisciplinary health team, and profession. Addresses patient welfare, advocacy, confidentiality, reporting obligations, and legal responsibilities. Requirements of the Code may exceed but never be less than those of the law.

AAPT is a nonprofit that administers national certification for psychiatric technicians at four levels (NCPT Levels 1-4). The code of ethics guides professional conduct of psychiatric technicians and is referenced in the certification framework. AAPT certification requires renewal every four years with 12 hours of continuing education. Organization provides ethics standards for mental health and developmental disability workers nationwide.

codes.document_title: Certified Nursing Assistant Code of Ethics
codes.notes: Widely recognized professional standards framework for CNAs. Based on fundamental values of worth, dignity, and uniqueness of all persons. Covers: CNA appearance and behavior, training and education (state-approved programs, CPR, certification exams), work performance (confidentiality, HIPAA compliance), patient care obligations, and reporting duties. CNAs obligated to report jeopardized patient welfare to charge nurse. Derived from ANA nursing ethics framework adapted for CNA scope of practice.

codes.document_title: Code of Ethics for Nurses with Interpretive Statements
codes.notes: First adopted 1950, most recently revised 2025. Nine provisions covering: compassion and respect for human dignity; primary commitment to patient; patient advocacy and rights; authority and accountability; duties to self; ethical environments; advancing profession through research; collaboration for human rights; social justice. Although primarily for registered nurses, the ANA Code is explicitly applied to CNA practice through the Nursing Education Advisory and Networking Team framework and serves as the foundational ethical reference for all nursing personnel including assistants and orderlies.

minor_groups.name: Occupational Therapy and Physical Therapist Assistants and Aides

codes.document_title: Standards of Ethical Conduct for the Physical Therapist Assistant
codes.notes: Adopted by APTA House of Delegates June 2009, effective July 2010. Eight standards: respect for dignity/rights; trustworthiness and compassion; sound decisions within PT supervision boundaries; integrity in relationships; legal and ethical obligations; competence and professional development; organizational behavior and business practices; meeting community health needs. Accompanied by the APTA Guide for Conduct of the PTA. In January 2026, replaced by a unified Code of Ethics for the Physical Therapy Profession combining PT and PTA standards.

codes.document_title: Code of Ethics for the Physical Therapy Profession
codes.notes: Adopted by APTA House of Delegates 2025, effective January 1, 2026. Unified code combining the former Code of Ethics for the Physical Therapist and the Standards of Ethical Conduct for the Physical Therapist Assistant into one comprehensive document. Core values: accountability, altruism, collaboration, compassion and caring, duty, excellence, integrity, and social responsibility.

codes.document_title: AOTA 2025 Occupational Therapy Code of Ethics
codes.notes: Originally adopted as AOTA 2020 Code of Ethics (American Journal of OT, 2020), replaced by AOTA 2025 Code of Ethics passed April 24, 2025. Applies to all occupational therapy personnel including OTAs and OT Aides. Provides aspirational Core Values and enforceable Standards of Conduct. OTAs work under supervision of and in partnership with occupational therapists. The AOTA Ethics Commission enforces the Standards of Conduct under Enforcement Procedures. Six core principles: beneficence, nonmaleficence, autonomy, justice, veracity, and fidelity.

Sets forth principles of ethical and moral conduct for medical assistants. Key principles: render service with full respect for human dignity; respect confidential information; uphold honor and high principles of the profession; seek to improve knowledge and skills; participate in community service. Accompanied by the Medical Assisting Creed for resolving ethical/moral issues. CMA (AAMA) credential holders must follow a separate Code of Conduct requiring high standards, accountability, fairness, and legal compliance. Violations can result in denial of certification.

codes.document_title: AAMA Code of Conduct and Disciplinary Standards for CMAs
codes.notes: Binding code of conduct for CMA (AAMA) credential holders. Requirements include: maintaining high standards, accepting responsibility for actions, being fair and honest, enhancing professional capabilities, following all applicable laws and regulations, and encouraging ethical conduct in others. Grounds for denial or revocation include felony conviction, professional license revocation, and AAMA disciplinary action. Distinct from the aspirational Code of Ethics.

codes.organization: National Association of Phlebotomy Technicians and Professionals (NAPTP)
codes.notes: Nine provisions: (1) compassion and respect for human dignity without prejudice; (2) primary commitment to the patient; (3) advocacy for patient rights, health, and safety; (4) authority, accountability, and responsibility for practice decisions; (5) duties to self including competence and growth; (6) maintaining ethical work environments; (7) advancing the profession through research, scholarship, and standards; (8) collaboration for human rights and health diplomacy; (9) articulating professional values and integrating social justice. Each provision accompanied by interpretive statements.

Founded 1983 as the second oldest national certifying agency of phlebotomy. Professionalism begins with the certification process. Core ethical obligations include: respect, patient advocacy, confidentiality, accountability, ongoing personal and professional growth, strict infection control procedures, maintaining a clean environment, never interpreting or disclosing lab results, and conforming to high standards of communication and conduct. Awards the PTC (ASPT) credential.

Adherence is prerequisite for AMTA membership. Key principles: commitment to highest quality bodywork; acknowledging inherent worth and individuality without discrimination; professional excellence through regular self-assessment and continued education; confidentiality and respecting client privacy; refraining from sexual conduct during massage sessions; providing only services within scope of practice and training; complying with applicable laws and regulations. Rules of Ethics are enforceable; violations subject to disciplinary action.

Members pledge to serve best interests of clients and provide highest quality bodywork. Key commitments: conduct thorough health history intake and evaluate for contraindications; obtain informed consent for session plan; respect client right to decline, modify, or stop session; maintain client confidentiality unless medically necessary or legally required; no dating clients, sexual activity, or sexual impropriety; provide only services within scope of practice and competence. ABMP is one of the largest massage/bodywork membership associations in the US.

codes.document_title: IAFC Code of Ethics for Chiefs
occupations_covered: 33-1021 First-Line Supervisors of Firefighting and Prevention Workers
codes.notes: Submitted by IAFC Ethics Committee, adopted by IAFC Board of Directors May 2003. Recognizes that fire chiefs serve in positions of public trust imposing responsibility to use publicly owned resources effectively and judiciously. Key principles: not using public position for personal advantage; using information only for public benefit; no conflicting outside employment; handling personnel matters on basis of merit; no commercial product endorsements for personal gain; developing and training personnel on ethical conduct. Part of IAFC Fire Service Professional Code of Ethics framework.

codes.organization: International Association of Chiefs of Police (IACP)
occupations_covered: 33-1012 First-Line Supervisors of Police and Detectives
codes.notes: Adopted at 64th Annual IACP Conference, October 1957; revised 2024. Fundamental duty is to serve the community, safeguard lives and property, protect the innocent against deception, the weak against oppression, and the peaceful against violence. Officers must respect constitutional rights of all to liberty, equality, and justice. Badge is symbol of public faith and trust. Paired with the Police Code of Conduct which provides enforceable mandates (acting impartially, exercising discretion, using only necessary force, maintaining confidentiality). The foundational professional ethics document for American law enforcement.

codes.organization: National Organization of Black Law Enforcement Executives (NOBLE)
occupations_covered: 33-1012 First-Line Supervisors of Police and Detectives
codes.notes: Founded September 1976 at symposium co-sponsored by Police Foundation and LEAA. Guiding principles serve as code of ethics: Uncompromising Integrity (conducting business according to ethical law enforcement standards); Courage of Convictions (proactively addressing controversial policies); Respect (for rights of all persons); Accountability (mutual between criminal justice system and community); Community Partnership (community integral to criminal justice); Value Diversity (throughout the criminal justice system). Mission: promote justice, equity, and excellence in administration of justice.

codes.organization: National Society of Executive Fire Officers (NSEFO) / Congressional Fire Services Institute (CFSI)
codes.notes: Product of almost two years of development by the NSEFO board (now IAFC EFO Section). Establishes criteria for promoting a culture of ethical integrity and high standards of professionalism. Key principles: never discriminate based on protected characteristics; never harass, intimidate, or threaten; be truthful and honest; report cheating or dishonest acts; not use position for personal gain; engage in no activities that could impair primary responsibilities. U.S. Fire Administration posted it throughout National Fire Academy facilities and incorporated into all NFA course materials. Individual firefighters encouraged to sign the Code.

Listed in IAFF Manual of Common Procedures. The IAFF, founded 1918, is a labor union representing over 340,000 professional firefighters and paramedics. Code of ethics covers member conduct and professional obligations. Addresses conduct unbecoming a member, with charges requiring specific terms. IAFF also committed to promoting positive human relations: every fire fighter regardless of protected characteristics has right to safe and respectful workplace. Separate conflict of interest provisions also apply.

Updated August 2018. Adapted from the National Firefighter Code of Ethics developed by NSEFO. Key requirements: be courteous, considerate, and civil; exercise utmost patience and discretion; avoid financial conflicts or perception of impropriety; not intimidate, bully, or threaten fellow members or public; refrain from behavior that reflects negatively on the fire service. Failure to comply may result in suspension or termination of NVFC membership.

Binding upon all NAFI members. Ten principles: (1) adherence to code; (2) impartiality regardless of characteristics; (3) regard profession as important and honorable; (4) inspire confidence of colleagues and public; (5) foster cooperation between agencies and public; (6) protect confidential information, no personal advantage; (7) continuously improve techniques and experience; (8) not work with those whose goals conflict with honest investigation; (9) make no false claims to qualifications; (10) be a fact finder seeking truth and accurate cause of fires/explosions. Accompanied by the Fire Investigator's Creed requiring honest and unbiased investigation.

IAAI founded 1949; all members required to uphold the Code. Focuses on maintaining high professional standards and eliminating factors interfering with administration of justice. Key principles: regard oneself as member of important and honorable profession; conduct personal and official life to inspire public confidence; exhibit professionalism and integrity in all duties; not use position for personal advantage or profit; respect fellow investigators' standards and confidences; know work thoroughly and pursue every opportunity to learn. Grievance procedure available for alleged violations. IAAI chapters worldwide maintain the code.

codes.organization: International Association of Chiefs of Police (IACP)
codes.document_title: IACP Law Enforcement Oath of Honor
codes.notes: Developed by IACP Committee on Police Ethics in 2000; revised by IACP Governing Body effective January 1, 2021, to emphasize treating all individuals with dignity and respect and preserving human life. Text: 'On my honor, I will never betray my badge, my integrity, my character, or the public trust. I will always have the courage to hold myself and others accountable for our actions. I will always uphold the Constitution, my community, and the agency I serve.' Available in five languages: English, Arabic, French, Spanish, and Portuguese. Designed as a shorter, more memorable complement to the full Law Enforcement Code of Ethics.

codes.document_title: Code of Ethics of the Office of Sheriff
codes.notes: Ten principles: (1) enforce and administer law according to U.S. and state constitutions ensuring equal protection; (2) establish and enforce employee conduct guidelines; (3) not tolerate or condone brutal or inhumane treatment of citizens or inmates; (4) maintain campaign integrity and adhere to election financing laws; (5) conduct regular audits of public funds; (6) apply management principles for efficient resource allocation; (7) merit-based hiring without bias; (8) adequate training and supervision for competent service; (9) avoid using office for private gain; (10) accept leadership responsibility for encouraging colleagues to uphold the code. Violation is grounds for censure, suspension, or expulsion from Association.

Adopted August 1994 by ACA Board of Governors and Delegate Assembly. Expects unfailing honesty, respect for dignity and individuality of human beings, and commitment to professional and compassionate service. Seventeen principles covering: civil and legal rights; welfare-centered service; collegial relationships and mutual respect; constructive criticism only; inter-agency cooperation; public information rights balanced with privacy; public safety; no position abuse; objectivity; conflict of interest avoidance; rejection of improper gifts; distinguishing personal/organizational views; reporting corrupt conduct; non-discrimination; information integrity; merit-based personnel decisions; safe workplaces.

codes.document_title: Code of Ethics for Jail Officers
codes.notes: Approved by AJA Board of Directors, adopted November 10, 1991; reaffirmed May 3, 2008 in Sacramento, California. Officers swear to be a good citizen and credit to community, state, and nation. Key principles: abstain from questionable behavior; lifestyle above reproach; perform duties according to laws and regulations; communicate professionally; contribute to jail environment keeping inmates in constructive activities; support professional development activities. Part of integral program to achieve high standard of professional conduct in the nation's jails.

codes.document_title: Code of Ethics for the Field of Community Corrections
codes.notes: APPA is an international association of individuals in probation, parole, and community-based corrections for both adult and juvenile sectors. Professionals recognize their office as a symbol of public faith and accept it as a public trust. Key areas: effecting social adjustment of offenders, conducting personal life with decorum, upholding the law with dignity, awareness of responsibility to community, objectivity in performance, respecting inalienable rights, appreciating inherent worth of individuals, and maintaining confidentiality.

codes.organization: Federal Probation and Pretrial Officers Association (FPPOA)
codes.notes: Revised March 11, 1993. Six principles: (1) professional service to courts, parole authorities, and community in effecting social adjustment of offenders; (2) personal conduct with decorum, no improper favors, loyalty to moral principles above personal consideration; (3) upholding the law with dignity and awareness of judicial system prestige; (4) objectivity, respecting inalienable rights, appreciating inherent worth of individuals, maintaining confidentiality; (5) cooperation with colleagues and partner agencies, continuous professional development; (6) viewing office as embodiment of public trust, sacred responsibility.

codes.organization: National Association for Civilian Oversight of Law Enforcement (NACOLE)
codes.notes: Adopted August 12, 2015. For civilian oversight practitioners overseeing law enforcement agencies, jails, and prisons. Key principles: transparency and accountability (regular reports and analysis); confidentiality (security of non-disclosable records); fair treatment (dignity and respect without discrimination including age, ethnicity, race, gender identity, housing status, mental health, religion, political beliefs); professional development (staying informed of legal, professional, social issues); impartiality; and independence. Practitioners earn trust through commitment to public good.

codes.organization: National Association of Emergency Medical Technicians (NAEMT)
codes.notes: Also listed under 33-9000 for EMTs. Included here because many law enforcement officers are cross-trained as EMTs and the code applies to all EMS practitioners working in law enforcement agencies. See entry under 33-9000 for full description.

codes.organization: National Association of Emergency Medical Technicians (NAEMT)
occupations_covered: 33-9098 School Bus Monitors and Protective Service Workers, All Other
codes.notes: Drafted by Charles Gillespie, MD; adopted 1978, revised June 14, 2013. Applies to all EMS practitioners (EMTs, paramedics, etc.) who fall under SOC 29-2040 but many are cross-classified under protective services. Eleven principles: (1) conserve life, alleviate suffering, promote health, do no harm; (2) provide equitable service without discrimination based on nationality, race, creed, color, or socioeconomic status, and not judge merits of patient's request for service; (3) avoid harmful applications of knowledge; (4) respect and hold confidential information; (5) use social media responsibly; (6) strive for clinical excellence; (7) support professional standards; (8) accept responsibility for professional actions knowing relevant laws; (9) engage in advocacy for EMS legislation; (10) cooperate professionally; (11) refuse unethical participation and expose incompetence.

codes.organization: National Registry of Emergency Medical Technicians (NREMT)
occupations_covered: 33-9098 School Bus Monitors and Protective Service Workers, All Other
codes.notes: Condition for NREMT certification and recertification. Requirements: comply with all NREMT policies including website Terms of Use; provide full, truthful, and updated information on all applications; adhere to highest standards of professionalism and ethics; act consistent with all federal, state, and local laws relating to EMS practice. NREMT maintains NCCA accreditation for four certification levels: EMR, EMT, AEMT, and Paramedic (NRP). Separate from but complementary to the NAEMT Code of Ethics.

occupations_covered: 33-9031 Gambling Surveillance Officers and Gambling Investigators
codes.notes: Aspirational code revised 2023 by global volunteer representatives. Six articles: (1) perform duties in accordance with law and highest moral principles; (2) represent services/products fairly and truthfully; (3) be faithful and diligent in professional responsibilities (fair, steadfast adherence to promises and best efforts); (4) be competent, not accepting tasks beyond competence or claiming unposessed competence; (5) safeguard confidential information, prevent improper disclosure, not use confidences to disadvantage of principal; (6) not maliciously injure professional reputation of colleagues, clients, or employers. Required affirmation for CPP/PSP/PCI certifications. ASIS represents 34,000+ security professionals worldwide.

occupations_covered: 33-9031 Gambling Surveillance Officers and Gambling Investigators
codes.notes: Companion to ASIS Code of Ethics. Enforceable code governing member conduct and professional practice. Revised 2023 alongside the Code of Ethics. Provides specific behavioral expectations for security professionals in areas including honesty, integrity, competence, and professional relationships. ASIS also offers the Certification Code of Professional Responsibility for certified security professionals (CPP, PSP, PCI, APP credential holders).

Non-profit established January 1988 to address training and certification needs of security/protection officers internationally. Ethical standards are core requirement for CPO (Certified Protection Officer) qualification: proctors must comply with code of ethics. Professional Security Officer Program (PSOP) covers professional ethics as required subject. Security Officers and Patrol Services Competency Model requires professionals to 'abide by a strict code of ethics and behavior, treat others with honesty, fairness, and respect, and make decisions that are objective and reflect the just treatment of others.' Ethics training integrated across all IFPO certification programs.

codes.organization: National Council of Investigation & Security Services (NCISS)
codes.document_title: NCISS Code of Ethics and Professional Standards
codes.notes: Set as standard bearer for investigative and security industry. Key principles: competence and diligence in professional services according to law; maintain competency in operating locales; honesty, integrity, and truthfulness in client dealings; honor client contracts; ethical services within limits of law; safeguard client confidential information; prevent unauthorized disclosure; not knowingly violate any individual right guaranteed by U.S. Constitution or state constitutions. Applies to regular members and NCISS leadership.

In 2023, NALI Executive Council adopted Code of Professional Conduct: Standards and Ethics for the Investigative Profession, 4th ed., by Kitty Hailey. Establishes high standard for legal investigation practice. Key principles: maintain highest professional standards with integrity, honesty, and excellence; afford all persons their rights and privileges; do not infringe on rights; truthfully represent services to public. CLI (Certified Legal Investigator) credential holders must adhere to this code. NALI organizes, serves, and educates members while enforcing professional canons of ethics.

codes.document_title: NACA Code of Ethics Statement and Code of Conduct
codes.notes: Key principles: perform duties impartially without bias based on status, sex, race, religion; maintain exemplary conduct to inspire community respect; use force only when necessary and reasonable to protect public, animals, or oneself; refrain from unnecessary infliction of pain or suffering; exercise discretion responsibly within the law (consider education before legal action); maintain confidentiality of information; avoid corruption or bribery; take responsibility for professional performance; continuously enhance knowledge and competence. Required for NACA ACO (Animal Control Officer) Certification.

codes.organization: Transportation Security Administration (TSA) / Department of Homeland Security
codes.document_title: TSA Employee Responsibilities and Code of Conduct (TSA MD 1100.73-5)
codes.notes: Federal management directive governing all TSA employees including Transportation Security Officers (TSOs). Requirements: perform duties professionally and in business-like manner; conduct not adversely reflecting on TSA on or off duty; uphold public trust with integrity; abide by 14 general principles of ethical conduct (5 CFR 2635.101) and DHS Supplemental Standards (5 CFR Part 4601). Annual ethics training provided (up to one hour of official duty time). Covers financial disclosure, outside activities, gift restrictions, and political activities. Accompanied by TSA Handbook and TSA Guide to Major Ethics Rules.

major_groups.group_name: Food Preparation and Serving Related Occupations
major_groups.sparsity_assessment: SPARSE — No unified industry-wide code of ethics exists. The American Culinary Federation provides the only occupation-specific professional code for chefs/cooks. Most food service workers are governed by employer policies, union contracts, and food safety certifications (ServSafe) rather than professional ethics codes. Bartenders have the USBG code of conduct; sommeliers have the Court of Master Sommeliers code. Catering has the NACE code. Supervisory roles lack separate ethics codes.

minor_groups.name: Supervisors of Food Preparation and Serving Workers
minor_groups.notes: No professional association publishes a code of ethics specific to food service supervisors. These roles are governed by employer policies and general food safety regulations. The National Restaurant Association does not publish a standalone code of ethics for the industry.

codes.notes: Binding on all ACF members and certified professionals. Covers compliance with public health/safety laws, non-discrimination in employment, prohibition on misappropriating property, duty not to harm colleagues through false statements, commitment to continuous learning and mentorship of peers. Ethics enforcement procedures allow fair review of alleged violations. ACF is the largest professional chefs' organization in North America with 14,000+ members.

codes.document_title: Code of Ethics and Professional Responsibility
codes.notes: Governs sommeliers who work in restaurants and food service (SOC 35-3031 Bartenders or related). Core values: Hospitality, Integrity, Humility, Self-Care, Diversity. Members must sign the code and complete safe-environment training. Covers non-discrimination, anti-harassment, anonymous ethics reporting. Updated post-2020 after independent investigation into sexual harassment. Cross-listed with 35-3000.

Founded 1948. Members must conduct themselves with honesty, integrity and fairness; support USBG values of Service, Integrity, Sharing Knowledge and Tradition; respect dignity and rights of others regardless of race, ethnicity, gender identity, sexual orientation, etc. Officers and employees must observe high standards of business and personal ethics.

codes.document_title: Code of Ethics and Professional Responsibility
codes.notes: Cross-listed from 35-2000. Sommeliers serve as beverage service professionals in restaurants and hotels. Core values: Hospitality, Integrity, Humility, Self-Care, Diversity. Mandatory anti-harassment training. Anonymous reporting via Lighthouse Services.

codes.organization: National Association for Catering and Events (NACE)
codes.notes: Covers catering and events professionals including food/beverage serving at events. Members must uphold laws of the land, conduct business with honesty, protect confidentiality, foster open and welcoming environment regardless of race/religion/gender/disability. Ethics complaints reviewed by Ethics Committee (ethics@nace.net). Cross-listed with 39-3000.

minor_groups.name: Other Food Preparation and Serving Related Workers
minor_groups.notes: Includes dining room attendants, hosts/hostesses, and food preparation workers. No professional association publishes a code of ethics specific to these roles. Workers are governed by employer policies, union contracts (e.g., UNITE HERE), and food safety regulations.

major_groups.group_name: Building and Grounds Cleaning and Maintenance Occupations
major_groups.sparsity_assessment: SPARSE — Building cleaning has trade association codes (ISSA, BSCAI) that target companies/contractors rather than individual workers. Grounds maintenance has the NALP code of ethics and ISA arborist code. Pest control has the NPMA code. Most individual janitors, maids, and groundskeepers are not subject to professional ethics codes — they operate under employer policies, labor contracts, and OSHA regulations. Supervisory roles lack separate codes.

minor_groups.name: Supervisors of Building and Grounds Cleaning and Maintenance Workers
minor_groups.notes: No professional association publishes a code of ethics specific to supervisors in this field. Supervisors are governed by employer policies and general industry standards from ISSA, BSCAI, or NALP depending on subsector.

minor_groups.name: Building Cleaning and Pest Control Workers

codes.organization: ISSA — The Worldwide Cleaning Industry Association
codes.notes: ISSA represents 10,000+ member companies in the cleaning industry worldwide. Members recognize obligation to serve public health and acknowledge responsibility to the industry. Code defines obligations and responsibilities for businesses acting professionally. ISSA also publishes Cleaning Industry Management Standard (CIMS) — the first consensus-based management standard for cleaning operations. Separate residential code exists at residential.issa.com/code-of-ethics/. Note: code targets companies/contractors, not individual janitors.

Covers 1,000+ member companies providing cleaning, facility maintenance, security, and landscaping services across 15 countries. Code addresses operating in accordance with best practices, professional standards, and ethical business conduct. Like ISSA, targets contractor companies rather than individual custodial workers.

All NPMA members agree to adhere to the code. Fundamental principles: integrity, honesty, professionalism. Members must maintain high company standards of responsibility, character and integrity; practice honesty and fairness in advertising and all client transactions; render skilled, intelligent and conscientious service; perform services safely and efficiently. Also includes anti-trust compliance and anti-harassment policies. NPMA represents 5,600+ pest management companies. 90+ year history.

codes.organization: National Association of Landscape Professionals (NALP, formerly PLANET)
codes.notes: Formerly Professional Landcare Network (PLANET), rebranded 2015. Members commit to: honest and scientifically accurate information; environmental protection and preservation; adherence to all contractual obligations and laws; fair treatment of subcontractors and suppliers; continuing education and certification; good safety practices; no recruiting competitors' employees at NALP events; equal opportunity regardless of race/color/creed/national origin. Covers lawn care, landscape management, design/build, and interior plantscaping.

Applies to all ISA credential holders and candidates (ISA Certified Arborist, ISA Certified Tree Worker, etc.). Establishes enforceable professional conduct standards and explains minimal ethical behavior requirements. Serves as central guide for day-to-day decision making, linking organizational values with professional conduct and industry standards. Arborists must have minimum 3 years full-time tree care experience. ISA has 30,000+ members in 50+ countries. Full PDF at isa-arbor.com/Portals/0/Assets/PDF/Certification/Ethics-Code-of-Ethics.pdf.

major_groups.sparsity_assessment: MODERATE — This is the most ethics-code-rich of the three groups, driven by funeral services (NFDA, ICCFA, CANA), personal appearance (cosmetology/barber state boards, beauty industry associations), animal care (NDGAA, NAPPS, IBPSA, IAOPCC), coaching (ICF), massage therapy (AMTA), and recreation (NRPA). However, many minor groups remain sparse: entertainment attendants (ushers, ticket takers), baggage porters/bellhops, and general personal care aides lack occupation-specific codes. Tour guides have the WFTGA code. Fitness trainers have ACE/NSCA codes.

minor_groups.name: Supervisors of Personal Care and Service Workers
minor_groups.notes: No professional association publishes a code of ethics specific to supervisors of personal care/service workers. Supervisors are governed by the ethics codes of their respective subsectors (e.g., salon managers follow cosmetology board standards, kennel managers follow IBPSA standards).

codes.organization: National Dog Groomers Association of America (NDGAA)
codes.notes: All NDGAA certified groomers must abide by the code governing business, customer relations, and advertising practices. Groomers promise to: accept responsibility when caring for all pets, enhance their beauty through proper grooming skills, continuously educate themselves and patrons in proper pet care and welfare, not discriminate against any person, and show affectionate understanding and gentleness while performing duties in a humane manner. Commitment to humane care, grooming excellence, fair business practices, and public health & safety.

codes.organization: National Association of Professional Pet Sitters (NAPPS)
codes.notes: The only national professional pet sitting association. All NAPPS members must adhere to the code covering animal welfare, client confidentiality, professionalism, and responsible pet care. NAPPS certification program committed to quality education on care and welfare of animals and sound/ethical business practices. Certified Professional Pet Sitter (CPPS) credential.

codes.organization: International Boarding & Pet Services Association (IBPSA, formerly Pet Care Services Association / American Boarding Kennels Association)
codes.notes: All IBPSA members must agree to abide by the code. Covers owners and employees of pet boarding and daycare facilities, groomers, dog walkers, pet sitters, veterinarians, trainers, and holistic pet care providers. Includes the Pet Owners Bill of Rights assuring pets will receive professional, loving care. Formerly ABKA (American Boarding Kennels Association), then Pet Care Services Association.

codes.organization: International Association of Pet Cemeteries and Crematories (IAOPCC)
codes.notes: Founded 1971. The only organization in the world to publish and uphold comprehensive Accreditation Standards in pet cremation aftercare. Members adhere to strict code established for the benefit and protection of the public, employees, members, and the association. Members represent the pinnacle of integrity and compassion in pet aftercare. Full PDF at cdn.ymaws.com/www.iaopc.com/resource/resmgr/code_of_ethics_edited.pdf.

minor_groups.name: Entertainment Attendants and Related Workers

codes.notes: Code of conduct for Certified Park and Recreation Professionals (CPRP). Covers ethical standards for parks, recreation, and leisure services professionals. NRPA has emphasized educating members about ethical behavior and violations of public trust. Relevant to recreation attendants, amusement park workers in park/recreation settings. Note: no code exists specifically for ushers, ticket takers, gambling dealers, or amusement/recreation attendants — these are governed by employer policies and, for gambling, by state gaming commission regulations.

minor_groups.notes: Includes gambling dealers (39-3011), ushers/lobby attendants/ticket takers (39-3031), and amusement/recreation attendants (39-3091). Gambling dealers are governed by state gaming commission regulations and casino-specific codes of conduct (e.g., AGA Responsible Gaming Code) rather than occupation-specific professional ethics codes. Ushers and amusement attendants lack any professional association or code.

codes.notes: Enforceable code effective January 1, 2004. Binding on NFDA members; violations subject to disciplinary action per NFDA Constitution and Bylaws. Five areas of obligation: (1) to families — professional, caring, respectful service, honest and fair dealings, consideration for those of lesser means; (2) to the deceased — highest respect and dignity, professional transport/preparation/shelter of remains; (3) to the public — highest principles of honesty, fair dealing, professionalism; (4) to government — compliance with laws; (5) to NFDA — upholding the association's standards. Full PDF at nfda.org/Portals/0/NFDAORG/About/Professional_Conduct/Code-of-Professional-Conduct.pdf.

codes.organization: International Cemetery, Cremation and Funeral Association (ICCFA)
codes.notes: Covers cemetery, cremation, and funeral service professionals internationally. 9,100+ member cemeteries, funeral homes, crematories, and memorial designers worldwide. Emphasizes dignity, transparency in pricing, and respect for diverse cultural and religious practices.

codes.document_title: Certified Cremation Specialist (CCS) Program — Ethics Module
codes.notes: CANA is a nonprofit trade association of 3,500+ members (funeral homes, cemeteries, crematories, suppliers). CCS certification includes ethics coursework covering personal and professional conduct, ethical decision-making, and dignity/respect in care of the deceased. CANA's primary focus is development and promotion of standards reflecting dignity and compassion. While not a standalone code of ethics, the ethics training is embedded in the credentialing program.

minor_groups.name: Personal Appearance Workers

codes.organization: American Barber Association (ABA) / American Barber Certification Council (ABCC)
codes.notes: Professional code for licensed barbers. Covers sanitation, client confidentiality, professional competence, and community responsibility. Part of the American Barber Certification Council (ABCC) program. Note: state cosmetology and barber boards also impose professional conduct standards as conditions of licensure, but these are regulatory rather than voluntary professional codes.

codes.organization: National Coalition of Estheticians, Associations, and Schools (NCEA)
codes.notes: Requires estheticians not to utilize any technique or procedure for which they lack adequate training. Must dress in attire consistent with professional practice. Covers scope of practice compliance, client safety, continuing education, and professional standards.

Members will only provide treatments for which they are fully trained and hold appropriate credentials. Will not work outside commonly accepted scope of practice for estheticians. Covers infection control per state/CDC/OSHA guidelines, client confidentiality, and adherence to state cosmetology board laws.
Code of ethics for nail technicians and manicurists. Covers professional conduct, hygiene, client safety, and ethical business practices in the nail care profession.

codes.document_title: Code of Ethics for Salon/Spa Professionals
codes.notes: Covers the broader beauty industry including hairstylists, cosmetologists, and salon professionals. Focuses on health and safety standards, hygienic practices (tool disinfection, clean workspace), truthful representation of services and products, client confidentiality, and ethical behavior. PBA is the largest organization of salon professionals, manufacturers, and distributors.

minor_groups.notes: State cosmetology and barber boards (e.g., California Board of Barbering and Cosmetology) impose regulatory standards of professional conduct as conditions of licensure in all 50 states. These are statutory/regulatory rather than voluntary professional codes but effectively function as enforceable ethics standards for the ~1.2 million licensed cosmetologists, barbers, estheticians, and nail technicians in the US.

minor_groups.name: Baggage Porters, Bellhops, and Concierges

codes.organization: Les Clefs d'Or (Union Internationale des Concierges d'Hotels, UICH)
codes.document_title: Les Clefs d'Or Code of Ethics and Professional Standards
codes.notes: International association of professional hotel concierges from 50+ countries, founded in France 1952. Members must annually sign an oath of continued adherence. Key standards: always respect and protect guest identity and confidentiality; listen attentively to requests; never accept goods/services from vendors for personal gain; Les Clefs d'Or USA concierges do not receive restaurant commissions nor participate in incentive-driven competitions; maintain professional appearance; never practice or permit discrimination. Two pillars: Service and Friendship. Note: no professional code exists specifically for baggage porters or bellhops — they are governed by hotel employer policies.

minor_groups.notes: Baggage porters and bellhops (39-6011) lack any occupation-specific professional code of ethics. These roles are governed by employer/hotel policies.

codes.organization: World Federation of Tourist Guide Associations (WFTGA)
codes.notes: Member associations accept the code on behalf of their guides. Key principles: provide professional service with care and commitment; provide objective understanding of the place visited, free from prejudice or propaganda; ensure that what is presented as fact is true, with clear distinction between truth and stories/legends/traditions/opinions; act fairly and reasonably with all who engage guide services and with colleagues; as representatives of host country, welcome visitors and bring credit to the destination. WFTGA Constitution Article 2 commits to promotion of high standards of training and ethics.

codes.organization: European Federation of Tourist Guide Associations (FEG)
codes.notes: European regional code complementing the WFTGA global standard. FEG represents tourist guide associations across Europe. Covers professional conduct, accuracy of information, client relations, and respect for cultural heritage.

minor_groups.name: Other Personal Care and Service Workers

codes.notes: World's leading coaching association. Four core values: Professionalism, Collaboration, Humanity, Equity. 28 ethical standards across four sections of responsibility. Covers confidentiality, conflict management, fair treatment, transparency, accountability, and anti-discrimination. 2025 revision adds AI use provisions — coaches must disclose use of artificial intelligence and ensure client interests are protected. Required for ICF membership and credentials (ACC, PCC, MCC). Full PDF at coachingfederation.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/icf-ethics-code-of-ethics-2025.pdf. Note: life/wellness coaches map to SOC 39-9099 (Personal Care and Service Workers, All Other).

Adherence is prerequisite for AMTA membership. Two sections: (1) Principles of Ethics (aspirational goals) — commitment to highest quality service, non-discrimination, regular self-assessment, continuing education, client confidentiality; (2) Rules of Ethics (mandatory, enforceable) — operate within scope of practice, refrain from sexual conduct with clients during sessions, truthful advertising, no misrepresentation of credentials/training/results. Violations subject to disciplinary action. AMTA is the largest massage therapy association with 75,000+ members.

Covers ACE Certified Personal Trainers, Group Fitness Instructors, Health Coaches, and Medical Exercise Specialists. Members promise: safe and effective instruction; equal and fair treatment; stay current on health/fitness research; maintain CPR/AED certifications; maintain client confidentiality; refer to more qualified professionals when appropriate; establish and maintain clear professional boundaries. Relevant to SOC 39-9031 (Fitness Trainers and Aerobics Instructors).

Covers NSCA-certified professionals (CSCS, NSCA-CPT). Must not misrepresent skills, credentials, or services; refer clients to more qualified professionals when appropriate; provide and maintain safe training environment free from abuse, harassment, or discrimination. Relevant to SOC 39-9031 (Fitness Trainers).

Industry-wide platform assuring clients of utmost professionalism in communication, confidentiality, privacy, and spa treatments. Directs behavior of both guest and staff in a mutually dignified and respectful manner. Spa facilities must meet requirements pertaining to staffing, safety, guest relations, and service per ISPA Standards & Practices to become members. Relevant to SOC 39-9099 workers in spa/wellness settings.

minor_groups.notes: SOC 39-9000 is a catch-all including childcare workers (39-9011), fitness trainers (39-9031), recreation workers (39-9032), residential advisors (39-9041), and personal care/service workers not elsewhere classified (39-9099). Childcare workers are covered by the NAEYC Code of Ethical Conduct (primarily educational, mapped to SOC 25-0000). Personal care aides who provide direct client care but are not licensed (e.g., home health aides) overlap with SOC 31-0000 (Healthcare Support) and are governed by employer policies and state regulations rather than professional ethics codes.

codes.document_title: Sales & Marketing Creed — International Code of Ethics
codes.soc_detailed: 41-1012 First-Line Supervisors of Non-Retail Sales Workers
codes.notes: SMEI founded 1935. Certified Sales Executive (CSE) designation requires adherence. Code mandates highest ethical and professional conduct in all business relationships with customers, suppliers, colleagues, competitors, governmental agencies, and the public. Members shall not participate in actions detrimental to customers or competitors.

codes.document_title: NADA Code of Ethics and Ethics Guide
codes.soc_detailed: 41-1012 First-Line Supervisors of Non-Retail Sales Workers
codes.notes: Ethics Guide covers four areas: sales, service, financial services, and advertising. Commits members to highest ethical standards, fair/open/honest treatment, clear product representation, and full compliance with anti-discrimination laws. Originally adopted 1963, updated 2017.

codes.document_title: NADA Code of Ethics — Sales Standards
codes.soc_detailed: 41-2031 Retail Salespersons
codes.notes: Sales-specific standards require embracing the spirit and letter of law governing retail sales of new and used vehicles, honesty and truthfulness with customers, and thorough product knowledge to satisfy transportation needs.

codes.soc_detailed: 41-2031 Retail Salespersons; 41-9099 Sales and Related Workers, All Other
codes.notes: Eight principles: Integrity, Respect, Fiduciary Duty, Compliance, Confidentiality, Loyalty, Duty, Excellence. Establishes per se violations (felony conviction, license revocation). Formal grievance procedure with 30-day response period.

codes.document_title: Code of Ethics and Standards of Practice
codes.soc_detailed: 41-3091 Sales Agents, Financial Services; 41-9022 Real Estate Sales Agents
codes.notes: One of the first codifications of ethical duties adopted by any business group. 17 articles organized around duties to clients/customers, public, and fellow REALTORS. Over 1.5 million members. Ethics training required every 3 years. Covers honest/fair dealing, avoiding misrepresentation, client confidentiality, prioritizing client interests, avoiding conflicts of interest. Updated annually.

codes.organization: National Association of Insurance and Financial Advisors (NAIFA)
codes.document_title: Code of Ethics / Ethics for Financial Professionals
codes.soc_detailed: 41-3021 Insurance Sales Agents
codes.notes: Founded 1890. Approximately 200,000 financial professionals. In July 2024, Board approved updated 'Ethics for Financial Professionals' incorporating FSP Code of Professional Responsibility. Covers client confidentiality, acting in clients' best interest, accurate/honest information presentation, and political advocacy for financial interests.

codes.document_title: ASTA Code of Ethics — Integrity in Travel
codes.soc_detailed: 41-3041 Travel Agents
codes.notes: 12-point code emphasizing 'Integrity in Travel.' Covers accuracy, disclosure of costs/restrictions/terms, credential integrity. Complaints filed with ASTA Consumer Affairs Department. Failure to adhere may result in disciplinary action.

codes.soc_detailed: 41-9022 Real Estate Sales Agents
codes.notes: Covers property management professionals (CPM designation). Requires holding proprietary information in confidence, maintaining accurate financial records, protecting owner's funds, loyalty to client interests. Where firm/client interests conflict, client takes precedence. Ethics and Discipline Committee enforces.

codes.soc_detailed: 41-9022 Real Estate Sales Agents
codes.notes: International standard. Over 140,000 members globally. Principles: honest/fair/transparent/professional conduct; due skill, care and diligence; fair terms of engagement; avoiding conflicts of interest; fair/clear/timely communications. Requires realistic price assessments based on professional judgment.

codes.organization: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA)
codes.document_title: Code on Interactions with Health Care Professionals
codes.soc_detailed: 41-3091 Sales Agents, Financial Services (pharma sales reps often classified here)
codes.notes: Originally published 2002, updated 2009, 2019, 2021 (effective Jan 2022). Promotes ethical relationships between pharma companies and HCPs. U.S. enforcement authorities view this as baseline for ethical interactions. Non-compliance used as evidence of misconduct under Anti-Kickback Statute.

codes.organization: Manufacturers' Representatives Educational Research Foundation (MRERF) / Institute for Professional Advancement (IPA)
codes.soc_detailed: 41-4012 Sales Representatives, Wholesale and Manufacturing, Except Technical and Scientific Products
codes.notes: Key principles: use only legal/ethical means in all activities; accept no personal compensation without employer's knowledge/consent; maintain confidentiality of privileged information; refuse to engage in activities for personal gain at company's expense; truthful/accurate communications; cooperation with industry colleagues. Certification holders must complete continuing education and pay annual dues while upholding code.

codes.document_title: AdvaMed Code of Ethics on Interactions with Health Care Professionals
codes.soc_detailed: 41-4011 Sales Representatives, Wholesale and Manufacturing, Technical and Scientific Products
codes.notes: Governs medical device/diagnostics sales representatives' interactions with HCPs. Originally 1993 (HIMA), relaunched 2003 as AdvaMed Code. Revised 2003, 2009, 2020, 2022. Addresses training/education, meals, grants, consulting arrangements. U.S. enforcement authorities view as baseline for Anti-Kickback Statute compliance.

codes.soc_detailed: 41-4012 Sales Representatives, Wholesale and Manufacturing, Except Technical and Scientific Products; 41-9091 Door-to-Door Sales Workers
codes.notes: Membership condition. Covers consumer protection (accurate product representations, documented earnings claims) and salespeople protection (90% buyback of unsold inventory within 12 months). Enforced by independent code administrator with power to decide remedies. Prohibits deceptive, false, unethical or unlawful practices.

codes.organization: World Federation of Direct Selling Associations (WFDSA)
codes.document_title: WFDSA World Code of Conduct for Direct Selling
codes.soc_detailed: 41-4012 Sales Representatives, Wholesale and Manufacturing, Except Technical and Scientific Products; 41-9091 Door-to-Door Sales Workers
codes.notes: First established 1985. All member DSAs must abide by the World Code. Covers consumer protection (prohibited practices, cooling-off periods, returns), treatment of direct sellers (recruiting, remuneration, earnings claims, repurchase). Based in Washington DC.

codes.document_title: Code of Ethics and Standards of Practice
codes.soc_detailed: 41-9021 Real Estate Brokers
codes.notes: See 41-3000 entry. Also applies to 41-9021 Real Estate Brokers. First adopted 1913, celebrated centennial in 2013. 17 articles covering duties to clients, public, and fellow members.

codes.organization: American Advertising Federation (AAF) / Institute for Advertising Ethics (IAE)
codes.document_title: IAE Principles and Practices of Advertising Ethics
codes.soc_detailed: 41-9011 Demonstrators and Product Promoters; 41-9099 Sales and Related Workers, All Other
codes.notes: Administered by AAF in partnership with Reynolds Journalism Institute and Missouri School of Journalism. 8 principles covering truthfulness, highest personal ethics in creating/disseminating commercial information, distinguishing advertising from news/editorial, and avoiding deception. Voluntary compliance.

codes.soc_detailed: 41-9099 Sales and Related Workers, All Other (Auctioneers)
codes.notes: See 41-2000 entry. Eight principles with formal grievance process and automatic per se violations for felony convictions or license revocations.

codes.soc_detailed: 41-9099 Sales and Related Workers, All Other
codes.notes: Certified Professional Sales Person (CPSP) certification emphasizes ethical sales practices as part of the psychology of selling, advanced sales strategies, and professional conduct. Specific code details available through NASP certification program.
